Question: How much better is the Gerald R Ford class of aircraft carriers over the preceding Nimitz class?
Answer: Incremental improvement. The two ships are structurally almost indistinguishable, aside from the Ford-class dropping an elevator that was never used underway anyway. The main difference is the electromagnetic aircraft launch system (EMALS) replacing steam catapults. It’s basically a railgun with a plane hooked to it. These have many fewer moving parts, meaning significant improvements in mechanical reliability. In other words, you're a lot less likely to get into a situation like what happened in the final battle of Top Gun where both catapults broke down at a critical moment, making it impossible for the Enterprise to launch any reinforcements after they sent up Maverick and Merlin. Skip to 2:40. Admittedly, this is deliberately a nightmare scenario brought on by a contrived coincidence of Hollywood, and therefore extremely unlikely in real life, but eliminating possible failure points is never a bad thing. The more common advantage of EMALS is significantly better control over launch acceleration curves: in other words, they can very precisely customize the boost to the aircraft and weather conditions. Steam catapults can't do this: they go at whatever speed they go at. Apart from EMALS, the main improvement over the Nimitz is an increase in automation, which cuts crew costs.

Question: Why should a black baker be forced to provide a cake for a KKK rally if the event doesn't matter in determining whether it is discrimination or not?
Answer: He shouldn’t. This is the key distinction from the case of the cake baker who refused to serve a gay wedding: by refusing to provide service to members of the Ku Klux Klan, the baker, whether they be white, black, or green, is not discriminating against others, but rather reacting to their discrimination. Furthermore, if that baker has employees, they also have a professional and legal obligation to provide them with a safe working environment where they’re not likely to be harassed by the KKK. Likewise, the bakery’s other customers expect a safe environment to shop without being harassed by the KKK. Freedom of speech is not freedom from consequences. Notwithstanding their history of domestic terrorism, the KKK are perfectly free to yell until they’re blue in the face about how brown people, Catholics, and Jews are ruining the country. And the rest of us are in turn perfectly free to call them the assholes they are and exclude them from civilized society, until and unless they choose to repent and start behaving like civilized people. People talk a lot about Karl Popper’s “paradox of tolerance”: that creating a tolerant society requires us to not tolerate intolerance. The truth is, Popper phrases it wrong: tolerance is not a moral principle, but rather a social contract. To wit, we collectively agree to treat each other like civilized people. Someone who refuses to do that is not adhering to the contract, and therefore is no longer protected by it.

Question: Why do most guitar amps have gain options, but not a lot (if any) have fuzz options built in?
Answer: Because of what fuzz actually is. This answer deals directly with how an electric guitar actually works. Nightwish guitarist Emppu Vuorinen with his signature ESP EV-1 six-string. An electric guitar works by picking up the sound produced by the strings in built-in microphones, then transmitting it, either through a cable or wirelessly, to an amplifier (“amp”) that increases (amplifies) the signal strength to where it is audible. This signal is then sent to a speaker, or more commonly to a soundboard that then sends it to the speakers. “Guitar fuzz” is what happens when this signal is distorted: in other words, fuzz is loss of signal fidelity. It was actually invented by accident in early vacuum tube-based amps: damage to the vacuum tubes caused a clean guitar sound to squeal instead, and artists thought this sounded cool so they started deliberately damaging them. Shortly after this, musicians such as blues guitarist Willie Johnson discovered they could produce similar sounds on an intact amp by powering it beyond its specifications, causing the peaks and valleys of the sound wave to be clipped. Chuck Berry went a different route on his 1955 single “Maybellene”: he used a cheapo amp that simply couldn’t accurately reproduce the signals his guitar sent it. Grady Martin is generally credited as the discoverer of “guitar fuzz”: a session guitarist on Marty Robbins’s 1961 hit “Don’t Worry”, he played with a fuzzy tone produced by a faulty preamplifier, then reproduced it on a solo instrumental song called “The Fuzz”. His recording engineer, Glenn Snoddy, then collaborated with a coworker, Revis V. Hobbs, to invent the “fuzzbox”, a standalone device to deliberately reproduce Martin’s fuzz effect, which they sold to Gibson Guitars. This was one of the first commercially successful guitar pedals. Guitar pedals like these are now the main way that rock and metal guitarists produce and control the distortion in their songs. It’s more convenient and more reliable than futzing with the amp itself, so there simply isn’t a market anymore for amps that do the distortion themselves. Vergere herself reappeared in a bit part as the familiar of Elan, a priestess of Yun-Harla, in Agents of Chaos I: Hero’s Trial (August 2000), later getting an expanded role in Jacen Solo’s character arc, and Zonama Sekot itself was found outside Chiss space in Force Heretic II: Refugee. Question: Would the clone troopers obeyed order 66, if they weren’t fitted with inhibitor chips?
Answer: Most would, some wouldn't. Which, believe it or not, is exactly what happened in the Legends continuity, where there were no inhibitor chips. The inhibitor chips were wholly an invention of the Clone Wars TV series, which de facto de-canonized the entire Clone Wars Multimedia Project long before the Disney takeover. Before that, in Legends, the clones made up their own minds. Believe it or not, this question speaks to a very real and important topic in military ethics: the duty to disobey an unlawful order. You see, in Western common law, there’s a longstanding tradition that the rules and regulations of the organization and the state take precedence over the wishes of any superior, even a King. Exhibit A: the Magna Carta, which the nobility of England forced King John Plantagenet to sign in 1215. While its actual effectiveness is debatable, it is often credited as introducing the concept of “rule of law”, rather than “rule of man”. If even a King is not above the law, then it logically follows that a King can give orders which are illegal, and therefore are not to be followed. Arguably the most famous expression of this happened in the post-World War II era at the Nuremberg war crimes tribunals, where the defense counsels of high-ranking officers of Hitler’s regime were banned by the court from using the so-called defense of superior orders, but it’s been around in fits and starts for centuries. I explore it in greater detail in this answer: Here’s where theory and practice collide, however: soldiers are trained to follow orders. Questioning orders isn’t something armies generally like, for reasons that should be fairly obvious. So, while ideally we would like a soldier to immediately refuse an order that is unlawful, in practice a soldier who receives an unlawful order often won’t even consider the lawfulness of an order, especially while keyed-up on adrenaline during combat or when an authority figure they generally trust gives it. It was for this reason that, contrary to popular belief, the post-WWII war crimes trials tended to cut more slack to more junior personnel: they were viewed as so dominated by their superiors that it was reasonable that, barring evidence to the contrary, they were assumed to not have been able to tell whether what they were doing was unlawful. In Star Wars, we further learned in Attack of the Clones that the Kaminoans genetically modified their slave soldiers to be less capable of independent thought than their baseline human donor, Jango Fett. Add to that a decade of highly regimented training and indoctrination, and you get a slave army that, while more able to improvise when things go wrong than the remote-controlled drones used by the Trade Federation et al., is not that capable of thinking for itself whether the orders they’re given are lawful. Which is fitting, considering that the very existence of a slave army is itself unlawful in the Republic. So what ended up happening is that most of the slaves received a “break glass in case of fire” order from their commander-in-chief—which Karen Traviss’s Republic Commando novel series not-unreasonably interpreted as part of a list of over 150 such orders,[1]because this is how such things tend to work in real military forces—and just obeyed what they believed to be a lawful order to frag their overseers. This was the explanation used in Matthew Stover’s much-loved Revenge of the Sith novelization. It’s also why the Jedi had so little warning despite their precognition: the slaves, by and large, bore little to no malice towards their overseers. They simply received what appeared to be a valid order, and obeyed it. With the Jedi Order overextended, spread thin across the galaxy, each Jedi is alone, surrounded only by whatever clone troops he, she, or it commands. War itself pours darkness into the Force, deepening the cloud that limits Jedi perception. And the clones have no malice, no hatred, not the slightest ill intent that might give warning. They are only following orders. In this case, Order Sixty-Six. Hold-out blasters appear in clone hands. ARC-170s drop back onto the tails of Jedi starfighters. AT-STs swivel their guns. Turrets on hovertanks swung silently. Clones open fire, and Jedi die. All across the galaxy. All at once. Jedi die.[2] But that isn’t the whole story in Legends. You see, not all the slaves were alike: while thinking critically was discouraged by the Kaminoans, it still had to be present to allow the slaves to “think creatively”. This was especially true of the higher-grade slaves: the clone commandos and the elite ARC Troopers. And this meant that contact with reality meant some slaves did think about it, especially when their Jedi overseers weren’t immediately at hand to shoot at (meaning more time to consider things). And they didn’t all come to the same conclusions. So again, the answer is: Most did, but some didn’t.

Question: Why are free-range eggs brown, but “ordinary” eggs are white?
Answer: They're not. The color of an eggshell is set by the breed of chicken. For example, white eggs you get from a grocery store are almost always from White Leghorns. They've been bred to produce a very consistently-sized white egg at regular intervals. It’s just genetics. This has a couple of advantages to egg sellers who produce industrial factory-farmed eggs: You can absolutely raise a free-range White Leghorn hen, but she will nevertheless still lay a white egg. Brown eggs have more variety. Rhode Island Reds are a common choice. We had them in our backyard flock when I was growing up, among others like Barred Rocs, Black Australorps, Turkens, and Buff Orpingtons. Rhodies lay big brown eggs, often oblong or with speckles. They’re also a fairly popular meat chicken: they have thicc thighs. As Franklin Veaux correctly notes in his answer,[1] industrial producers of so-called free-range eggs wanted a way to visually distinguish their product from the supposedly inferior indoor chickens that produce white eggs, so they went with brown egg breeds. But these are still a far cry from true free-range birds: often it’s just a small outoor pen. Industrial farms have even been recorded not even allowing them out of a barn: it’s an improvement over being stuck in a layer cage 24/7 but not by that much.[2] Other chickens lay in even stranger colors. Araucanas are a family of South American breeds known for laying bright blue eggs. They frequently have tufts of feathers around the face or neck. If you cross an araucana with a North American brown egg breed, you get what’s been called an Americana or Ameraucana. Ours laid pale brown or green eggs. What you’re effectively doing by crossbreeding the chickens is jumbling their genetics, making them more like their more diverse ancient ancestors. All modern chickens, Gallus gallus domesticus, descend from a Southeast Asian bird species called the red junglefowl, Gallus gallus. A prolific egg-layer just like modern chickens, humans switched from hunting them to capturing and raising them for food about 8,000 years ago.[3] True junglefowl lay eggs in all colors of the rainbow, but typically they come in pale to dark brown shades. Just like we’ve done with dogs and other livestock animals, humans have since used the art of selective breeding to produce chickens with traits that we find more useful for our purposes. But there’s ultimately no way to actually tell just by looking at the egg shell whether it came from a true free-range bird. What you instead have to do is look at the egg yolk. That orange color of the egg on the left isn’t food dye: it came out of a very happy, healthy hen that was allowed to live as God intended. Our backyard birds were allowed to forage freely on 23+ acres of lawn and scrubby forest, plus kitchen scraps, whatever seed got knocked out of our bird feeders by clumsy mourning doves, and the odd egg that broke in handling (yes, chickens will be cannibalistic given the opportunity). Sometimes when they were pullets, we’d see them chasing June bugs around the yard trying to catch them out of the air. They got a lot of exercise and were very well-fed on a very diverse diet, so they laid big, orange-yolked eggs, and on the rare occasions we butchered one, we got very lean, brown meat: if I didn’t know better I would have sworn I was eating turkey. That is how you know a true free-range chicken. Fun fact: There are an estimated 26.56 billion chickens in the world, which makes them the most numerous animal on the entire planet, humans included.[4]

Question: What genre is it if the story has its own worldbuilding without magic or sci-fi?
Answer: Speculative fiction. “Speculative fiction” is basically the umbrella term for anything that isn’t 100% based on real life: sci-fi, fantasy, horror, you name it. Here’s some examples: Ace Combat Most of the Ace Combat combat flight simulator series takes place in the world of “Strangereal”, so named because it’s definitively not Earth, but is basically the same as our Earth technologically, even down to having most of the same military aircraft. It was formally created to be the setting of Ace Combat 04: Shattered Skies, with the three preceding games being retconned to take place in it. Altina the Sword Princess This novel series by Yukiya Murasaki takes place in a world loosely based on Europe circa 1600, where pikes and cavalry are slowly giving way to cannon and musket. The center of the continent is dominated by the powerful and expansionist Belgarian Empire, loosely inspired by France at the height of its power, whose mad philanderer of an emperor is slowly running it into the ground with his constant wars and obsession with birthing a male heir with the red hair and eyes and freakish strength of the semi-legendary Empereur Flamme who founded the dynasty. Unfortunately for him, those traits instead went to his third child, Princess Marie Quatre Argentina de Belgaria, “Altina” for short: a now-teenaged girl sired on a common-born concubine, who is ordered to take command of a regiment holding the northern border against barbarian tribes and the independent Duchy of Varden because her father is sick of being reminded she exists. There are some fantastical elements—the super-strong “fairy steel” from which the heirloom weapons of the Empereur Flamme were forged, and the fact Altina can swing a zweihander taller than she is around like a toothpick—but there’s nothing in the series that’s explicitly magical: the drama is all based on the internal and external politics of Belgaria and the surrounding countries as Altina vies for the throne against her half-siblings and defends it against foreign counterattacks, hoping to take power for the sake of commoners like her mother.

Question: Did Latin have several dialects like ancient Greek?
Answer: Yes! The modern family of so-called “Romance languages”—whose name directly denotes Rome as the origin—are all descendants of regional dialects of vulgar (common) Latin, plus varying degrees of admixture of “barbarian” tongues, such as Gothic, Frankish, or Slavic. That's why you can get by throughout much of Europe if you speak one of them: so much of the vocabulary and structure is similar because they all have Latin at their core. One of the big reasons English is weird as a language is that it is not a Romance language at heart: rather it's basically Dutch, a northwestern Germanic language, but with about half the vocabulary replaced with formal Catholic Church Latin and Norman French—which itself is vulgar Latin mixed with Frankish and Norse. There have been various attempts to reconstruct a language more like Old English minus the Latin influence, generally called “Anglish” after the so-called Anglo-Saxons who might have spoken it today if they hadn't been thrown out of power by the Normans in 1066.

Question: Is Dungeons & Dragons popular in Japan, or do they play a different TTRPG?
Answer: I don't know precisely how popular D&D is in Japan, but yes, it is heavily played and has been extremely influential on their popular media. Most of the stereotypical Japanese fantasy setting traces its ancestry to Japanese geeks making glorified fan fiction of their campaigns. The media franchise Record of Lodoss War rather famously began life as a novelization of an original-setting D&D Basic Set campaign that creator Ryo Mizuno ran for some friends in the 1980s. Mizuno went on to create a rules-agnostic setting book for Lodoss (it predated the creation of the Open Gaming License), then retconned Lodoss into the world of Forcelia where his 2d6-based Sword World RPG is set. More recently, D&D directly inspired the novel series Goblin Slayer and The Faraway Paladin. In the original novels, the world of Goblin Slayer is literally a tabletop RPG being played by the gods of the world, and even though the anime cut this subplot, you can still hear the sound of dice being rolled occasionally. Even without that, the D&D influence is quite blatant if you know what to look for: The spellcasters frequently mention how many spells they have left (D&D’s classic “Vancian” magic system), and the “giant eye” the main party fights in the capital city sewers is obviously a beholder (they just couldn’t call it that without getting permission from Hasbro). The setting started as a thought experiment by the author on a gaming forum: “What if there was an adventurer who only fought goblins?” The author of Saihate no Paladin discusses his love of D&D partly giving rise to the setting (along with the Western fantasy literature that itself gave rise to D&D) in the first novel’s afterword, but it’s pretty obvious. William G. Maryblood is a paladin in the classical mold: a “warrior priest” empowered by his patron god to smite evildoers and lay the dead to rest, but only to protect others who lack his might and skills.

Name: Aaron Davis
Question: Is General Grievous pure evil?
Answer: No. Which isn't to say he's secretly a nice guy. Grievous, nee Qymaen jai Sheelal, was a general of the Kaleesh people, a fairly obscure Outer Rim race known for wearing masks of bone and practicing ancestor worship: they believed the most legendary among them in life would become gods. Some time before the Clone Wars, Grievous was a leader in the defense of Kalee against a race called the Huk. After driving them off of Kalee, he led a counterattack against the Huk homeworld and put it under military occupation. The Huk, annoyed at having done to them what they’d done to the Kaleesh, decided to play sore losers and appealed to the Republic and the Jedi. Typically for the Republic of the prequels, they and the Jedi took the side of the Huk: they ejected the Kaleesh from the Huk homeworld and put them under economic sanctions, causing a famine that killed hundreds of thousands. The InterGalactic Banking Clan hired the Kaleesh as mercenaries in exchange for paying off the war reparations the Republic had forced on them. When Grievous tried to back out of the deal to mount reprisals against the Huk for desecrating Kaleesh shrines on former colonies, they and Count Dooku arranged for him to suffer debilitating injuries in a shuttle crash in order to place him in a cyborg body they could more easily control. The conspirators framed the Jedi for the fatal crash, which was all it took to get Grievous on board with destroying the Republic and killing every Jedi within reach. So yeah, he's still a villain, but he's a pitiable one with a sympathetic origin story, not just a total psycho.

Question: How do you deal with finding actual evidence that a creator of media that you genuinely enjoy and find comfort in is a genuinely horrible, problematic person and hasn’t changed?
Answer: I find other media to consume. You can see from my credential that I used to be a huge Potterhead. I dressed up as Harry Potter for Halloween when I was ten, when only the first three novels were out. I wrote a bigger answer about why people have turned on Rowling a few years ago, but the short version is, her very public turn to trans-exclusive radical feminism (TERF) led to me reevaluating the books. So I went and found other books to read that weren’t written by a queerphobic, classist asshole. One of the ones that really hooked me recently was, of all things, a Japanese light novel series. It’s called Reign of the Seven Spellblades, penned by Alderamin on the Sky author Bokuto Uno. There’s also a manga adaptation by Sakae Esuno (creator of Future Diary) and an anime adaptation of the first three volumes that aired in the Summer 2023 season. The Harry Potter influence on this series is very strong, but there’s a lot of key differences. Quite apart from the presence of multiple openly queer characters, the series often reads like Bokuto-sensei was thinking to himself, “Hey, what if we took this thing people have criticized about Harry Potter because Rowling was clueless, and made it a deliberate feature of a dystopia?” Consequently, the core conflict of the series is much more “Man versus Society” than “Man versus Man”. Mages as a whole are obsessed to an often unhealthy degree with pushing the boundaries of magic, and as a direct consequence this world sucks to live in almost as badly for mages as it does for nonmagicals and demihumans. Some want this to change, but many don’t: Headmistress Esmeralda practically brags in her opening address to the freshman class that one in five of them will be dead, “consumed by the spell”, before their seven-year course of study is complete. So rather than pit the protagonists against wizard neo-Nazis attacking from outside, the enemies are all right there in the school: part and parcel of the fucked-up system everyone’s trapped in, not malcontents trying to overthrow a merely flawed world from outside. Mage children are victimized in traumatic generational cycles by mage families trying to get ahead, nonmagicals are second-class citizens at best, and intelligent nonhumans are third-class if they’re lucky: one of the professors laments the fact she’s not allowed to snack on centaur livers anymore because the reformists are starting to actually make forward progress. And the main character, Oliver Horn? Well, best not spoil that…[1] I do similar things with other media. Question: Why was Darth Vader so feared by the Jedi?

Question: Why didn't TIE Fighters have a hyperdrive and shields to begin with?
Answer: They didn’t need them. Remember the words of General Omar Bradley: “Amateurs study tactics; professionals study logistics.” The Empire as a state has a very good logistical situation. Your basic “eyeballs”, to use the Rebel parlance, are cheap to build, and they’re fast and very maneuverable, and they fit extremely well into Imperial doctrines. No proton torpedoes? Who needs those when we have star destroyers? No hyperdrive? Again, who needs those when we have star destroyers? TIE Fighters are designed to be tied to a carrier vessel or a base, because the Empire has plenty of those. They don’t need anything heavier because their mothership hauls them to the conflict zone and can step in if they run into problems. And they're small and lightweight enough that anything the size of a Corellian corvette or bigger can carry a few, even if they have to use up a few cargo airlocks as docking points to do it. Plus, as the Empire lost popularity, the lack of a hyperdrive proved to have a secondary advantage: it made it harder for their pilots to defect to the Rebellion a la Viktor Belenko in 1976. The lack of deflector shields is harder to defend from a moral standpoint, but, again, it boils down to logistics: not having deflectors saves mass. The eyeball’s defense is its speed and maneuverability. And frankly, the Empire has nothing even close to a peer opponent to deal with anymore: most of their enemies can easily be wiped out with sheer numbers and the eyeball outperforms everything commonly in civilian inventories. The Empire can easily conscript a dozen pilots and build a dozen equally cheap eyeballs to replace every individual one the Rebels, some pirate or Hutt enforcer, or Hapan daredevil manage to kill. Thing is, the eyeball was designed for a particular time and logistical scenario. The advantage of numbers fell apart after the Battle of Endor and the rise of the New Republic, and basic TIEs became much more vulnerable: the shielded, missile-armed heavy fighters of the Rebellion proved far deadlier when they could afford to blow previously precious proton torpedoes and concussion missiles to “thin the herd”. Ultimately, Grand Admiral Thrawn himself, no longer able to easily replace his losses, started ordering his eyeballs equipped with aftermarket deflector shields.

Question: What was Palpatine's opinion of Padme Amidala?
Answer: She was a useful idiot. This term is often attributed to the Soviets during the Cold War or to Vladimir Lenin specifically, but is actually at least as old as 1864.[1] It refers to a person in politics who believes they are fighting for a cause, without fully comprehending the results of their actions or that they’re being manipulated to do things useful to another political player.[2] In The Phantom Menace, Palpatine has a very simple, straightforward plan: For this plan, Padmé Amidala, née Naberrie, isn’t even a useful idiot: she’s just a political prop, “the brave queen forced to knuckle under to a foreign invader to save her people”. However, he can’t predict everything, and gets outmaneuvered when Velorum gets the Jedi involved. Not only do Qui-Gon Jinn and Obi-Wan Kenobi succeed in getting off the ship after he tries to have them killed, they even rescue Queen Amidala and bring her to Coruscant to blow the whistle on what his current useful idiot Nute Gunray is doing. So he adjusts: he gets her to propose Velorum’s removal. She thinks she’s doing the hard but right thing by selling out a political ally to save her subjects. She has no idea she’s being used by the Dark Lord of the Sith in an electoral coup. That’s the only value Sheev Palpatine, “Darth Sidious”, sees in anyone at all: their use as a tool for his own advancement. Something similar happens in Attack of the Clones. A full year ago when the film begins, somebody in the Senate proposed that the Republic reauthorize the federal armed forces, which had been abolished since victory in the last Sith War a thousand years earlier. This would allow the Republic not only to put down the Outer Rim Separatist movement should it turn violent, but also actually enforce the federal laws that the megacorporations and their droid armies are openly defying. But Padmé Amidala thinks all militaries are automatically bad, even though it was her own homeworld’s effective lack of one that made it vulnerable to being taken hostage by the Trade Federation to extort the federal government, and the Republic's lack of one that let the Trade Federation get away with it. Paradoxically, she’s convinced that the Republic’s demonstrated inability to keep the peace is actually good thing. Once again, that’s useful to Palpatine. He’s got his own irons in the fire for his long-term plan: he’s secretly building an army of his own beyond the Outer Rim, using money embezzled from the Republic and the megacorporations. Here’s the problem: it’s not ready yet. There’s a full year left in the cloned slaves’ growth and indoctrination timeline before even the first batches are ready for primetime. If the Republic creates an army now, it will create one that he can’t control: a lawfully obtained army composed of volunteers and conscripts that will be much less reliable when it comes time to purge the Jedi. So he uses Padmé Amidala, the irrational hoplophobe still wedded to the good ol’ days of a Republic that could actually govern rather than accepting the current reality that it refuses to, to obstruct the Military Creation Act until he’s good and ready for it to actually pass. Once he’s got a good eight divisions’ worth of slaves and a fleet ready, then he can get it authorized. At that point, Padmé shifts from being a help to a hindrance: the army is ready, the Seps are ready to fight it, and now her refusal to get her allies in the Senate to pass the bill is getting in his way. So he agrees to let his apprentice Darth Tyranus, a.k.a. self-proclaimed CIS head of state Dooku, have her killed as a sop to his ally Gunray. Huh, weird. Okay, let’s try that again. Of all the kriffing— Okay, at least she’s off Coruscant. Now he can pass the damn bill. And this way he even got emergency powers in the bargain, because Jar Jar Binks is an even bigger idiot than Padmé.

Question: Why would anyone do their car's oil change themselves when it's really cheap if taken to an expert's workshop?

Question: What is a good romance light novel recommendation with no harem?
Answer: Rascal Does Not Dream of Bunny-Girl Senpai Okay, so I’m stretching the “no harem” criterion a bit, but it’s more of a “monster of the week” series. Male lead Sakuta Azusagawa is a loner plagued by rumors of having put classmates in the hospital in middle school, with only a couple of actual friends: basketball jock Yuuma Kunimi and science nerd Rio Futaba. One day, as he’s hanging out in the local library, he sees a teenage girl dance through the room wearing a Playboy Bunny costume—and realizes he’s the only one who can see her. The girl’s name is Mai Sakurajima, a fairly well-known child actress who quit after, so it’s rumored, a fight with her manager/mother. After which, she began to realize that more and more people were becoming unable to perceive her, and forgetting that she had ever existed. This is the core conceit of the series: Adolescence Syndrome, a phenomenon where teenage angst collides with quantum mechanics to cause strange things to happen in the macro world. Sakuta falls hard for Mai, and begins working tirelessly to try and help her before she disappears from the world completely—then ends up having to do the same thing for various other girls in later books, variously including his kouhai Tomoe Kouga who causes a Groundhog Day-style time loop, his friend Rio who creates a doppelganger of herself, and his own younger sister Kaede who lost her memory and has become a shut-in due to cyberbullying. But throughout the series it’s made abundantly clear that Mai is the only girl for him, which is mutual: while Tomoe has a crush on him, Rio’s problem actually stems from her unrequited feelings for their mutual male friend Kunimi. Anime trailer: Reign of the Seven Spellblades This is a heavily Harry Potter-influenced dark fantasy series by Bokuto Uno (creator of Alderamin on the Sky). Main character Oliver Horn, a freshman at the prestigious Kimberly Magic Academy in the land of Yelgland, forms a bond of friendship with five other students when they work together to rescue one of their number after a troll goes berserk at the opening ceremonies. This bond will prove both boon and complication, because he came to Kimberly carrying secrets darker than the labyrinth below. While there are multiple characters interested in Oliver romantically, it would be wrong to call it a harem: I prefer the term “love dodecahedron”, since the series’ structure has more in common with a Western teen drama like Smallville, than a straight-up harem series. The romance plots form a complicated and constantly evolving web of relationships with Oliver at the center, and it’s not just girls since queerness and polyamory are relatively accepted among mages. His primary love interest is Nanao Hibiya, a former samurai from the faraway land of Yamatsu plucked from the losing side of a battle by a Kimberly instructor, who connects spiritually with Oliver when they spar on the first day of class. The series takes its time developing their relationship—which is complicated by the fact that Nanao is unable to separate her romantic attraction to him from her desire to finish their duel, to the death—but they do ultimately get together in volume 10 (of a presently unfinished series likely to run for over twenty volumes, with each school year comprising three or four). Anime trailer: Unnamed Memory Adapted from a web novel originally published on Shousetsuka ni Narou, this is another dark fantasy series. Under circumstances yet to be elaborated, Oscar was cursed along with his father as a child by the Witch of Silence: any woman either of them impregnates will not survive the event, which is a big problem when you’re the crown prince of the Kingdom of Farsas. To prevent a succession crisis that could potentially destroy the kingdom, Oscar seeks out the Witch of the Azure Moon, said to grant one wish to anyone who reaches her living quarters at the top of her tower. Oscar succeeds, and asks the Witch, a woman named Tinasha, to lift the curse. She informs him that she can’t do it immediately because the spell is simply too complex, and she doesn’t know how long it will take, but a backup plan would be to find a woman with sufficient magical resistance to withstand it. To which Oscar suggests that she do it: become his consort and the mother of his heirs. Understandably, she balks at this, and they negotiate down to Tinasha coming to Farsas for a year as his court mage, during which she’ll work to break the curse and he’ll attempt to woo her properly. The novels have an interesting structure, with Tinasha herself being the real protagonist, and the characters are quite complex and flawed: Oscar is simultaneously a highly competent man who takes his obligations as the future king very seriously, and a still-immature young man who is deeply smitten with Tinasha and, to put it delicately, doesn’t really know how to take “no” for an answer. Tinasha, meanwhile, does like and trust him, but she very much has her own agenda that doesn’t include a husband. The anime adaptation is ongoing, but it cuts a lot of chapters from the books so I can really only recommend it as a preview of the series: you lose a lot of material that develops the relationship between Oscar and Tinasha more fully.

Question: What were the main differences between Darth Vader's TIE Fighter and a regular one? Why did he have additional features on his fighter?
Answer: Darth Vader’s bird of choice was a TIE Advanced x1. The TIE Advanced was a Sienar Fleet Systems prototype heavy fighter. It had similar armament to a standard TIE/In Fighter but more crew features. The TIE Advanced was a close competitor to the T-65 X-Wing, but standard TIEs were good enough for most purposes—and were also harder for pilots to defect with as the regime’s popularity waned, since they lacked hyperdrives. The TIE Advanced never saw wide use except by elite and politically reliable pilots (including Darth Vader), and was largely superseded by the TIE Interceptor. However, it can be seen as a forerunner of some later TIE variants, particularly the TIE Defender, which had similar features and addressed the shortcomings of its engines.

Question: Why in the 80s, everyone could believe in a Mach 2.0 helicopter like Airwolf, but nowadays they don’t?
Answer: Nobody serious believed it then, either. Something you may have forgotten: according to the show, the Airwolf couldn’t break the sound barrier with just its rotors. It required a jet engine with an afterburner to break the sound barrier. Let me repeat that: not a jet turboshaft engine like the Bell 222 that the chopper in the show was built from, but an actual freaking jet engine. The difference being, a jet turboshaft engine uses a jet turbine in place of, say, a piston engine or an electric motor, to power the rotor shaft, much like an Abrams tank uses a jet engine to power its own systems. Whereas in a fixed-wing jet aircraft, the jet engine itself provides the propulsion. The Airwolf is basically cheating to go supersonic, and even that is just a handwave. It works because the script requires it to do so, no other reason.

Question: Do you guys have some manga, manhwa, or manhua based on otome game with interesting plot? The MC can be heroine, villainess, mob, or maybe one of the love interest.

Question: Could you "program in pure machine code" by manually writing out bytecode in a .bin file and then running it? If it's of any importance, I'm using Ubuntu Linux. Would this work?
Answer: Sure. Why would you want to? This an MSP430 development board from Texas Instruments, similar to the one I’ve used in class at NC A&T. It has a 16-bit ARM microcontroller in it that you program with the Micro USB port in the upper-right corner and TI’s IDE, Code Composer Studio. Now, you can’t write straight-up machine code for this using the standard methods, but you can do the next best thing: assembly language. This is the level of programming that the IDE converts into machine code. Alternatively, you can write in a high-level programming language, namely C (the 1989 standard by default; you can also use the 1999 or 2014 standards with some adjustments). High-level programming languages are representations of assembly language, which your coding environment compiles into assembly language and then assembles into machine code. This is a very simple program to procedurally divide one number by another number using C, reading the memory using the development environment. I had to do this for a lab assignment in my Introduction to Microprocessors class. This is the equivalent program in MSP430 assembly language. See how much longer that is? Each one of those lines of assembly language equates to a single instruction in machine code, and even discounting the stuff off the top and bottom that were included in TI’s assembly template (lines 1–25 and 58–68), it’s still more than twice as long as the C program. And even here, it’s still somewhat legible: you can see, for example, that I’m doing some arithmetic (e.g. add, dec), that I’m doing some jumps (jge, jmp), and designating some memory space for variables (Dn: .short 40). In-line comments certainly help but they’re not that necessary. Now, these are some machine language instructions for the ARM processor architecture that this MCU is based on. Question: What is the last thing to happen in Star Wars: Legends?
Answer: There’s two answers to this question. By in-universe chronology, the answer is Star Wars: Legacy, Volume II. The Sith came back again in the form of the One Sith, led by Darth Krayt. They were defeated after warring with the Fel Empire and the Galactic Federation of Free Alliances for several years, at which point the Empire, Alliance, and Jedi Order established a triumvirate to act as a sort of United Nations between them. After their defeat, the One Sith went into hiding to attempt to rebuild, but started getting hunted by Darth Wredd, an admirer of Darth Bane who wanted to reestablish the Rule of Two. This indirectly drew in Ania Solo, a non-Force-sensitive Skywalker descendant who ran a junk shop in the fringe worlds, who got tangled up with an Imperial Knight whose master had been killed by Wredd. By real-world chronology, Star Wars: The Old Republic is still running and producing content, making it the only ongoing Legends work. Earlier this year EA shifted development duties to Broadsword Online Games to free up BioWare to refocus on its bread-and-butter single-player RPGs, including Mass Effect 5 and Dragon Age: Dreadwolf. As of the 7.4.1 release, there’s been a lull in the forever-war between the Sith Empire and the Galactic Republic: both are still recovering from the war with the Eternal Empire of Zakuul, and are mostly engaged in smaller-scale skirmishes. In this gap, there’s been a new development. Shae Vizla, a.k.a. Mandalore the Avenger, took over after Mandalore the Vindicated was killed in the Zakuul conflict, and has been pushing significant reforms as the Mandalorians continue their evolution away from the semi-nomadic Crusader era towards their prequel-era portrayal as a settled clan culture that prizes martial readiness rather than violence itself. Shae has recently been challenged on this by Heta Kol, the self-proclaimed Field Marshal of the Hidden Chain, who opposes her reforms and is mounting a civil war to seize the mantle of Mand’alor and return the Mandalorians to the marauding conquerors whom the whole galaxy feared. Most recently, the two leaders fought over the world of Ruhnuk, then got involved in the civil war on Ord Mantell that’s been going on since the start of the game.

Question: Could a paladin accept the validity of a pantheon of deities? Wouldn't that amount to a fundamental and therefore fatal confusion as to the ‘One True Path’?
Answer: It depends on the particulars of the setting. This is actually a worldbuilding question rather than a rules one. Since at least 3rd Edition it’s been possible in RAW for divine spellcasters, paladins included, to follow causes rather than deities. Some settings don’t allow this: Forgotten Realms and Pathfinder require all divine spellcasters to have a patron deity. In Eberron, on the other hand, per the rulebooks (I’m basing this on Faiths of Eberron from 3.5E), it is not even certain that the gods even exist. The polytheistic Sovereign Host and Dark Six faiths exist side-by-side with the henotheistic Silver Flame faith (it accepts the existence of multiple gods but only worships one), as well as the completely atheistic Blood of Vol mystery cult (a religion that holds that the only divinity in the world exists within mankind itself). The Church of the Silver Flame is probably closest to what you’re looking for, but there’s other odd variants: some atheistic religions in Eberron can support paladins according to RAW. The Path of Inspiration and Path of Light philosophies, followed by the Quori, are both Lawful Neutral, and the Undying Court is an elven religion of ancestor worship tagged as Neutral Good. In Pathfinder Second Edition, the Prismatic Ray is a trinitarian religion that venerates the goddesses Shelyn (love, beauty, and the fine arts), Desna (freedom and travel), and Sarenrae (healing, fire, and the sun) equally. Under 2E rules you can make a paladin that worships the holy threesome (there’s a longstanding bit of lore that they’re in a polyamorous relationship). Shelyn, Desna, and Sarenrae. Art by Klaher Baklaher.[1]

Name: Aaron Davis
Question: How many galaxies are there in the Star Wars universe?
Answer: That depends on how you define “the Star Wars universe”. We know in both Legends and Disney canon that there are some other galaxies within striking distance of the Galaxy Far, Far Away. The GFFA is a big one, much like our own Milky Way, and like ours, it has several dwarf galaxies orbiting it. One of them, the Rishi Maze, is described in Attack of the Clones: the Kamino system is said to be 12 parsecs (39 light-years[1]) outside it, which places the star in the galactic halo rather than within the galaxy proper. In Legends, the Outbound Flight project was intended to colonize another galaxy, though which one is unknown. There were also four known cases of travelers arriving in the GFFA from another galaxy. The Silentium, Abominor, and Yuuzhan Vong, as well as the living planet Zonama Sekot (the offspring of the original Yuuzhan Vong homeworld Yuuzhan’tar) all arrived from the same galaxy: the Silentium, Abominor, and Yuuzhan Vong first fought a three-way war that ended in the two droid species being driven out, then the Yuuzhan Vong fell into civil war and ultimately rendered their entire home galaxy uninhabitable. The fleet that invaded in 25 ABY was all that was left of their race, or at least that’s what we’re told. The total number of galaxies in the Star Wars universe is completely unknown. If it’s like our universe, “hundreds of billions” is a likely estimate.

Question: What was the last time a Jedi encountered a Sith before the Sith revealed their continued existence in the Phantom Menace?
Answer: A few days earlier. Shortly before the Naboo Crisis, a Coruscanti information broker named Lorn Pavan acquired information from a Trade Federation dissenter that could potentially unravel the first stage of Senator Sheev “Darth Sidious” Palpatine’s planned coup against Supreme Chancellor Finis Velorum. Darth Maul was sent to clean up the mess. At the same time, Darsha Assant, a Padawan on her trial to be promoted to Knight, was tasked with exfiltrating a Black Sun informant. In a misadventure, the informant accidentally fell to his death, and Assant and her master, Anoon Bondara, agreed to confirm it before reporting her failure to the Jedi Council. The two happened to run into Pavan and his droid I-5YQ fleeing Darth Maul, who had gotten Pavan’s name from the dissenter before killing him, and engaged him in battle. Maul overpowered Bondara, who blew himself up by stabbing the power supply of Maul’s speeder with his lightsaber to cover Assant’s escape. Maul spent the next several hours pursuing Assant, I-Five, and Pavan through the underlevels of Coruscant’s hive city. Assant eventually sacrificed herself to cover up Pavan’s escape, but Pavan gave his incriminating information to Senator Palpatine without knowing he was the Sith assassin’s master. Maul then killed Pavan in the hospital where he was recovering from his injuries, giving him a quick death as a show of respect for the trouble he gave him. By this point, the Naboo Crisis had begun. I-Five, however, escaped, and, following the declaration of the Galactic Empire, found his way to Pavan’s son Jax, a Jedi Padawan who had managed to evade Order 66 and started a business as a private detective.

Question: Besides Ilum, what other planets in Star Wars Official Related Continuity along with Legends can Sith or Jedi find Kyber Crystals to create their lightsabers?
Answer: Kyber crystals weren't even a requirement in Legends. Lightsabers instead used focusing crystals that could be found basically anywhere or synthesized in high-pressure chemical reactors. Corran Horn used a Corellian Durindfire gem he was given as a bribe by Moff Leonia Tavira to be her boytoy as the primary crystal for his lightsaber. He had a second one, a synthetic Kubaz xurkonia, offset to create an optional longer blade, but the low-quality crystal burned out the first time he used it. Tenel Ka Djo made her first lightsaber using crystals recovered from a lava tube on Yavin 4. Unfortunately, the crystals were too flawed: her lightsaber failed during training and her arm was accidentally severed by Jacen Solo and then exploded. She built her second one using higher-quality gems she extracted from her Hapan princess regalia. Jacen Solo originally used a corusca gem recovered from the depths of the gas giant Yavin. This crystal was cracked during the Yuuzhan Vong War, and Jacen replaced it with a lambent—a crystalline Yuuzhan Vong organism that gives off light, which enabled Jacen to sense Yuuzhan Vong and their creations with the Force. Jaina Solo handcrafted her focusing crystals in a pressure chamber, because she was a science nerd. She unknowingly rediscovered the process commonly used by the Sith to make lightsaber crystals, meaning that her blade turned out red in color. (She's usually drawn with a purple blade to avoid confusing people on her alignment.)

Question: Was the B-17 really tougher than the B-24, or any other 4-engined bomber for that matter? Or is this just a myth? If true, what was it that the B-17 had that other bombers didn't, that contributed to its ruggedness?
Answer: Yes. There are several things that contributed to the B-17 being a tougher aircraft, and preferred by aircrews for it. Now, loss rates for the two planes were about the same: 1.16 per 1,000 sorties for a B-24 versus 1.66/1000 for a B-17. This is simply because the combat conditions didn’t differ from one plane to the other: they were doing the same missions and faced the same densities of anti-aircraft fire and interceptor aircraft. But the loss rates don’t tell the whole story. Planners preferred the B-24 because it could take a bigger load of bombs further. Aircrews preferred the B-17, because if God forbid you were in one of the 1.66 sorties out of a thousand where the plane had to be written off, you were more likely to walk away from the incident. B-17s regularly made it home with practically half the plane missing. One such incident even made it into a Sabaton song, after a German fighter pilot named Franz Stigler couldn’t bring himself to finish off a B-17F piloted by Lieutenant Charles Brown, Ye Olde Pub.

Question: Is there any non-force-related story/fiction in the Star Wars Universe? Would it work at all, like a sitcom in Naboo or a detective in Coruscant?
Answer: Star Wars: X-Wing. Written in multiple installments from 1996 to 2012 by Michael A. Stackpole (of BattleTech fame) and Aaron Allston, this novel series was instrumental in creating the modern idea of an expanded universe as we know it. This was not the first Star Wars novel series by any stretch, but it was one of the first to attempt to actively tie preexisting material together into a single more-or-less coherent continuity Prior to this series, Star Wars novels and comic books were written mostly independently, but Stackpole and Allston actively collaborated and frequently made reference to earlier-written novels. The Lucasfilm Story Group didn’t come about until way later, largely as a result of Stackpole getting tapped to be the designated continuity wonk on the planning committee for The New Jedi Order. X-Wing does all this without featuring any Jedi or Sith: only two major characters are even Force-sensitive. Rather, this series is straight-played military science-fiction that happens to be set in the Star Wars universe, revolving around the regular New Republic Defense Force, specifically Starfighter Command. The series begins two years after the Battle of Endor: the Banite Sith have been defeated for good and the Empire is in disarray, but Luke Skywalker remains the galaxy’s sole active Jedi Knight and is still learning how to rebuild the Jedi Order, and the New Republic is still basically a military junta with aspirations rather than a functioning democracy. As the allied fleets prepare to invade the Core Worlds with the goal of taking Coruscant, Commander Wedge Antilles, the Republic’s ace of aces, is trying to reconstitute Rogue Squadron, first commanded by Luke Skywalker in the years between A New Hope and Return of the Jedi. He seeks to create an elite special operations group: starfighter pilots who can double as special warfare officers for the most complex strike missions. The first four novels cover the campaign to first capture Borleias, then Coruscant itself, as the Rogues struggle against the machinations of Ysanne Isard, Director of Imperial Intelligence and dictator of the largest Imperial Remnant faction. This is mostly seen through the eyes of an original character, Corran Horn, a former Corellian Security Force officer who defected to the Rebellion after a dispute with Imperial Intelligence, and, unbeknownst to him until book three, the grandson of a Corellian Jedi Master killed in action late in the Clone Wars. However, he doesn’t start actually training as a Jedi himself until way later, in the spin-off novel I, Jedi (which forms a quasi-trilogy with Timothy Zahn’s The Hand of Thrawn). This is followed by three books by Aaron Allston, which act as a prequel to the 1994 novel The Courtship of Princess Leia. Fresh off the campaign to liberate Thyferra, where Isard (seemingly) made her last stand after the fall of Coruscant, Wedge makes a bet with Admiral Ackbar: that he can take the misfits, failures, and dregs of Starfighter Command and forge them into a second functioning special operations group, this time focusing on the commando side of the equation. If Ackbar decides it’s a failure, Wedge has to accept his long-delayed promotion to general (don’t ask, Star Wars rank systems are weird) and join Ackbar’s staff—meaning leaving the cockpit. Each novel focuses on a different aspect of what is dubbed “Wraith Squadron”, as they fight to take down the new biggest dog in the Imperial junkyard, Warlord Zsinj. The first follows primarily Kell “Demolitions Boy” Tainer, the son of a man whom Wedge’s XO Wes Janson had to shoot down to keep him from blowing a mission. The second switches perspectives to the squadron’s fast-talker, Garik “Face” Loran, and the third stars Wedge himself in collaboration with Han Solo, who takes command of the task force sent to bring down Zsinj’s super star destroyer Iron Fist and break the back of his power once and for all. The next three novels are standalones. Isard’s Revenge skips ahead a couple years to the end of Timothy Zahn’s The Last Command: Grand Admiral Thrawn is dead and the Empire is on the back foot again, and the New Republic decides to invade the Ciutric Hegemony to keep it that way. Rogue Squadron is back in the foreground and Corran Horn has the starring role again, but Ackbar has finally guilt-tripped Wedge into accepting his promotion, so this is his last campaign as a front-line pilot. Starfighters of Adumar is another Wedge novel. Two years after the much-maligned Jedi Academy trilogy by Kevin J. Anderson, Qwi Xux dumps Wedge, who has a mid-life crisis and starts to consider retirement, but instead gets tapped to serve as an ambassador to the backwater planet Adumar, whose large indigenous arms industry could give the Republic an edge in the forever-war with the Imperial Remnant. Admuar idolizes fighter pilots, so Wedge leads three of his best friends—Wes Janson, Hobbie Klivian, and Tycho Celchu—to Adumar to win their support, clashing with the Empire, the nutty indigenous politics, and a rogue Republic diplomat who is determined to gain Adumar’s allegiance at any cost. In the midst of all this, Wedge rekindles his long-stalled romance with Iella Wessiri, a former coworker of Corran's from CorSec who is now a Republic intelligence officer. The last novel, Mercy Kill, takes place following the Fate of the Jedi series, and has the distinction of being one of the last Legends novels published before Disney shut the continuity down. The Republic, now the Galactic Federation of Free Alliances, has been at peace with the rump of the Empire for decades, but a conspiracy in the high command threatens to upend this and reunify the galaxy under Imperial rule (in the sense of the Palpatine-era Empire, rather than the relatively more enlightened oligarchy it became under Admiral Pellaeon’s tenure as military dictator), so a new generation of Wraith Squadron goes into action to root out the conspiracy and restore the peace. Stackpole and Allston, incidentally, were good friends both with each other and with Timothy Zahn, and before Allston’s death in 2014 they would often do joint convention appearances as "The Aaron, Mike, and Tim Show".

Question: Does is seem like all of the third party TTRPGs are really just systems trying hard not to be 5e, in hopes they can grab some of the market? Are there any that are not just rebranded 5e, trying to be the next Pathfinder following D&D4e?

Question: Which Sith in Star Wars has the highest body count?
Answer: Darth Vitiate. (answer previously posted here) The three faces of evil. Left to right, Tenebrae of Nathema, Emperor Valkorion of Zakuul, and Sith Emperor Darth Vitiate. A disfavored bastard son of the Sith warlord who ruled the remote planet Nathema, the young man born with the name Tenebrae delved deeply into the study of Sith sorcery while feuding with his old man. The conflict drove him to ever greater heights, culminating in him performing a ritual that drained all life and even the presence of the Force itself from the entire planet, leaving it a dusty, lifeless husk, and transforming Tenebrae into a bodiless, life-consuming intelligence of the dark side. Over subsequent centuries, Tenebrae marauded across the galaxy, taking various powerful Force-users as host bodies, consuming their minds and Force essences. As Darth Vitiate, he reunified and rebuilt the Sith Empire of Marka Ragnos, and drove Mandalore the Ultimate to launch a crusade against the Siths' ancient enemies: the Galactic Republic and the Jedi Order. Dozens of worlds including Cathar were burned in the Mandalorians' efforts to provoke the Republic to war. Ultimately a schism developed in the Jedi Order, which still keenly felt the losses from the unrelated Great Sith War only decades earlier: when the Jedi Council refused to intervene, fearing Jedis' fall in the war and suspecting something far more sinister than battle-crazed Mandalorians was going on, a young Knight named Revan led what Jedi would follow him to war anyway. Taking up the faceplate of a Mandalorian who died trying to stop her comrades from massacring civilians, Revan and the so-called “Revanchists”, including his friends Alek and Meetra Surik, took command of the Republic's armed forces and ultimately dealt the Mandalorians a defeat from which they never truly recovered. However, the war took a toll. The compromises necessary to fight a war made the Jedi vulnerable to the dark side, as the Council had feared. Revan and Malak (as Alek now called himself) pursued the fleeing Mandalorians back where they came from: the Kaas system, where Darth Vitiate awaited him. Vitiate easily defeated the renegade Jedi, twisting and torturing them until the survivors were fully in the embrace of the dark side. He proclaimed them Dark Lords of the Sith and dispatched them to take the Mandalorians’ place in making war on the Republic. It didn't work as well as he hoped: twisted though he'd become, Darth Revan retained enough sense to know that Vitiate was an existential threat to life itself, and built his war strategy around conquest of the Republic to place himself atop it so that he could turn the superpower's industrial might against the Sith Empire. He failed. In the meantime, Vitiate was formulating a new plan, having found a better tool for his plans than the fractious Imperial Sith. The remote planet Zakuul had become wealthy and powerful on the back of technologies looted from a long-dead precursor race, and Vitiate took over and hollowed out their emperor, a man named Valkorion. Taking no chances, he ordered the Sith Empire to launch a full-scale attack on the unprepared Republic. The war lasted years and featured innumerable atrocities, culminating in an all-out assault on Coruscant itself by Darth Malgus and Darth Angral even as peace negotiations took place between the Supreme Chancellor and Darth Vengean. The Coruscant Jedi Temple itself fell to the invaders before Republic reinforcements gained the upper hand. Within twelve years, the war hawks among the Sith got their wish: provocations along the border forced the Republic to declare war. Unlike the first time around, the Republic gained the upper hand almost immediately: several prominent Dark Councilors were killed in the early stages, either by the Republic or by internal struggles they couldn't end fast enough, leaving the pragmatic veteran warrior Darth Marr and the upstart, unorthodox sorcerer Darth Imperius as de facto co-rulers. Then Darth Vitiate himself suffered a setback: a Republic strike team of special forces and Jedi Knights landed on Dromund Kaas itself and managed to kill his host body there. The Emperor's spirit was badly injured and fled. After months of hard fighting, the duumvirate of Marr and Imperius managed to stabilize the front, only for the Order of Revan, a splinter cult that had formed after Revan's first war, to come out of left field. Darth Revan himself, more than a little cracked from three centuries as Vitiate's chew toy, led the way, but was foiled in his attempt to get Marr and Jedi Grandmaster Satele Shan to wipe each other out over Rishi Prime. Marr, Shan, and their allies called a truce and pursued Revan to Yavin 4. Having failed at Rishi, Revan gambled the last of his strength on reawakening the wounded Vitiate, hoping to kill him for good. It backfired. Revan gave up: 300 years of battles had taken their toll, and he passed his struggle against the Emperor on to the current generation and became one with the Force. Vitiate, however, fled Yavin, revitalized by the deaths of the Republic, Sith, and Revanite forces in his vicinity, and made a pit stop on the Imperial world Ziost, where he drove the inhabitants mad en masse before eating that world like he had eaten Nathema. He then resumed full control of Valkorion, and dispatched the Eternal Fleet and the Knights of Zakuul under the command of Valkorion's sons Arcann and Thexan in a bloody sweep of the Republic and the Empire, demanding their subservience. Darth Marr and his ally—Darth Imperius as far as I'm concerned—were taken prisoner attempting a counterattack, and the Republic and the Empire were forced to surrender. Marr was killed by Valkorion in a failed escape attempt before Imperius managed to kill Valkorion, assisted by his surviving son Arcann, who then turned on her as well and froze her in carbonite—unaware that Tenebrae had body-surfed into Imperius herself. Five years later, Imperius was freed by her allies Lana Beniko and Theron Shan. The subsequent war with the Alliance they forged saw Zakuul's hegemony collapse under the misrule of Arcann and his insane sister Vaylin. Vitiakorion hoped to mold Imperius into his new host, but miscalculated: experienced at battling malevolent Force ghosts, in the end she finally managed to kill him when he tried to hollow her out as well. Question: While playing a paladin, have you ever run into a roleplay-related problem because of your code of conduct or oath?
Answer: My current paladin PC, Fiorina N.A. Mazzanti, has had several occasions where her vows have been a source of conflict. This is a Pathfinder 1E game, War for the Crown, so she starts with the basic D&D3.5E/PF1E code of conduct[1] and then adds some custom stuff based on her patron goddess—Shelyn, NG goddess of romantic love, beauty, and the fine arts—and the Oathbound Paladin subclass, of which she has two oaths: The Oath of Love hasn’t been a huge issue (it’s come up a couple of times but never unfavorably), but the others have caused a lot of interesting situations. Fiorina grew up in Infernal Cheliax until she was about seventeen: the tomboy daughter of a Kintargo baron, she was disowned for getting pregnant out of wedlock and insisting on keeping the baby, and was rescued by the local clergy of Shelyn, then emigrated to the Republic of Andoran. As a young adult, she embraced both Shelyn’s cult and the democratic precepts of Common Rule with all the zeal of a new convert: the other players have been known to jokingly call her “Captain America”. Image credit: Hijabi Hooligan Cosplay[5] And this poses quite a few problems in the campaign’s setting of Taldor: the rump state of what used to be the Inner Sea Region’s version of the Roman Empire, it’s a feudal state that has been stuck partway into transitioning to a constitutional monarchy for several centuries. Having been born a noblewoman, she can empathize with the perspective of the local aristocrats on popular democracy, but she certainly doesn’t agree with them. Her campaign hook is that she’s working for the Andoren foreign intelligence service, the Twilight Talons: with Taldor on the verge of a succession crisis, her orders were to ensure that the throne passed peacefully to a candidate who would keep the peace with Andoran, meaning Princess Eutropia Stavian. She, however, dreams bigger, and—her original cover as a minor noble from the north having been blown in part one of the campaign—has been trying to persuade Eutropia to commit to creating a House of Commons in the Imperial Senate. This went about as well as you’d expect, at least initially: Eutropia quite literally laughed in her face and called the idea of commoners voting absurd. She moved on to discussing her plans to prevent a civil war by politically defeating the other claimant, her cousin Arch-Strategos Maxillar Pythareus, and asked for our support. The other PCs agreed to follow her lead, but Fiorina took a long dramatic pause—and at that point the GM and the other players got a little nervous and I had to stop and reassure them I was just roleplaying: I wasn’t going to blow up the campaign just because the main quest-giver said ‘no’ to my character. In-character, Fia reluctantly agreed to table the discussion of a House of Commons for the time being, but she did refuse to make any kind of loyalty oath to the Princess. So the other PCs who didn’t already have Taldan noble titles got knighted, but she didn’t (not that she cared, already being an Andoren Eagle Knight in her own right). So that was the Oath of the People’s Council causing an issue. Her religious vows to Shelyn were always present a little bit—for example, I normally at least attempt to take prisoners by inflicting nonlethal damage when fighting humanoid opponents—but they became a fairly large issue when we were attacked by a trompe l’oeil—a living painting, basically. We beat it, but actually disabling it permanently would require the destruction of the canvas, according to the statblock. So naturally everybody looks at the paladin of the art goddess. I told them that since the painting had literally just tried to kill us, it wasn’t against my vows to destroy it, but I’d prefer if we could find a different solution. So the GM had the arcanist PC roll Knowledge (arcana), which he did pretty well at, and told him that he could deactivate the trompe l’oeil by messing with the spell inscription on the back of the canvas that the GM totally didn’t just make up. (We collectively decided that he drew a dick over it.)

Question: Why didn't the New Republic care about the First Order, and how strong it was getting?
Answer: Stupidity. Out-of-universe, it was the stupidity of these two bantha-kriffers: Kathleen Kennedy’s mismanagement of Lucasfilm—in particular, her complete lack of an actual coherent vision for the trilogy beyond dollar signs—gave J.J. Abrams a free hand to simply revert the conflict to Rebels vs. Empire so he could remake the Original Trilogy with bigger explosions, because he doesn’t have an original bone in his body. The New Republic going from a reasonably competent state in Legends to a galactic cranial-rectal inversion in Disney canon is simply the logical consequence of that, as written by authors who thought a hell of a lot further about this bantha-poodoo sandwich they’d been handed than the cooks that made it. The New Republic couldn't be competent or else there wouldn't be a need for the “Resistance”, just the New Republic Defense Force. In-universe, it came down to the politics that birthed the Alliance to Restore the Republic. The Rebel Alliance was a coalition of many factions who really only agreed on wanting Palpatine’s Empire plain gone. Beyond that, they all wanted different and mutually exclusive things: Unfortunately, the first two groups outnumbered the third. The restorationists, like Mothma, got it into their heads that with the Imperial armed forces all but defunct after the Battle of Jakku, there was no need for them to maintain their large military any more—meaning they could cut taxes for themselves—and they were only too willing to forgive and forget with ex-Imperial personnel. Together with the ex-Separatists, they worked together to create a New Republic government that was even less effective than the late Old Republic, a truly impressive feat: Mothma’s people were happy that they had a government that didn’t superficially resemble the Empire in the slightest way, like actually trying to govern, and the Separatists were happy that Coruscant was at least staying out of their hair. And meanwhile, just like the US government after the Civil War, they both allowed their government to be thoroughly infiltrated by unreformed fascists, who diverted resources to the Imperial Remnant and helped ensure the reform faction wasn’t listened to when they tried to sound alarms. The inevitable result? A constitutional suicide pact, courtesy of one of those Imperial Remnant factions managing to get ahold of part of Sheev “Superweapon-of-the-Month” Palpatine’s collection. Compare that with the real New Republic that writers with actual talent spent 25 years writing about before Disney shit all over them. The Legends NR certainly did its share of dumb things, but it kept its military active and functional, and sincerely worked to provide effective governance and regulation. And as a direct consequence it remained in power with only a few brief interruptions for over a hundred years and counting, even finding a genuine detente with a thoroughly reformed Empire.

Question: Is there any great manga, manhwa, manhua, or novel where an OP MC struggles to control their power?
Answer: World's End Harem: Fantasia. This is the first spin-off of Shuumatsu no Harem, this time set in a dark fantasy setting instead of a post-apocalyptic one, and runs in Shueisha’s seinen magazine Ultra Jump. Seven Seas does the English translation. The star is this guy, Arc d’Lazharl Nargala, the teenaged heir to the County of Nargala, a minor realm on the eastern edge of a continent menaced by the tyrannical and expansionist Madalis Empire. Arc falls in love with his second cousin, Aurelia of House Isteshia, who’s promised to the Imperial crown prince to seal a nonaggression treaty. They try to elope, but are caught, and Arc is thrown in his father’s dungeon for the night to cool off. Which is when he’s visited by a mysterious, scantily clad dark elven sorceress named Latiforiazhard (“Lati” for short, and the cover girl for volume 1), who offers him the power to make the world his oyster. Following a forbidden ritual that infuses him with the essence of a black dragon, any woman who partakes of his blood becomes unable to live without periodically consuming his bodily fluids (sweat, saliva, blood, and semen all work equally well), and both he and she gain great magical powers. Somewhat unusually for the “slave harem” trope (which has become depressingly common of late), the series fully considers the ramifications of such a power. While “Macht” (German for “power” or “authority”, and somewhat amusingly, a feminine noun) is Arc’s greatest weapon against his enemies—which include both the Empire and members of his own family, particularly his great-uncle Arges, Count Isteshia—he agonizes a lot over the moral implications. If not managed well, mostly by adding women to his harem to spread it out, the power has a risk of overrunning his will and causing him to become uncontrollably aggressive: the first time this happens, he forcibly rapes his maid Wenna (cover girl of volume 3), impregnating her, and isn’t much mollified when she tells him she enjoyed it. He also starts to become more cognizant as the series goes on of the fact that, to some extent, he’s overriding the free will of the women he feeds his blood to, and is disturbed at times by his increasing willingness to enslave non-consenting women to achieve his goals. (Though karma seems to have an opinion on it, too: the most recent times he’s tried it, it’s backfired on him spectacularly.)

Question: How do you intrigue players to invest in a political intrigue plot line surrounding war, and what rewards/incentives would you consider giving them?
Answer: Make it personal. One of the pitfalls of writing grimdark war storylines is that you can focus too much on the large-scale hostilities and the deaths of thousands, and forget what it’s doing to people. Warhammer is sometimes a serious offender here: we get all kinds of talk about how the Imperium is a hellhole that’s slowly losing and how the bells of Holy Terra constantly toll for the deaths of heroes. It can be very impersonal. Which, to be fair, it was a tabletop wargame first. One of the things that has drawn people to the Black Library novel series, like Ciaphas Cain and Horus Heresy, is that they’re very personal stories. In Death or Glory, Cain comes to a town in the aftermath of an ork WAAAGH! moving through, and imagines scenes of horror: the orks butchering civilians in the streets purely for sport. In general, Sandy Mitchell is very good at being subtle about the grimdark so that it sneaks up on you: he uses lots of little touches, like offhand mentions of children’s books about burning heretics and running them over with tanks. The Heresy, too, has very personal stakes, that also translate out to the wider conflict: you feel every bit of how the Primarchs’ love for their brothers was torn asunder by their clashing priorities, for example the confrontation between the Wolves of Fenris and the World Eaters in Betrayer, where Angron accuses Leman Russ of hypocrisy in offering worlds “freedom” only at the point of a million boltguns, and calls out the Emperor’s fascism for what it is. “You are free, Leman Russ of Fenris, because your freedom matches the Emperor's will. For each time I wage war against worlds that threaten the Imperium's advance, there comes another time when I am told to conquer peaceful worlds that wish only to be left alone. I am told to destroy whole civilisations and call it liberation. I am told to demand millions of men and women from these new worlds, to make them take up arms in the Emperor’s hordes, and I am told to call this a tithe, or recruitment, because we are too scared of the truth. We refuse to call it slavery. “I am loyal, the same as you. I am told to bathe my Legion in the blood of innocents and sinners alike, and I do it, because it is all that's left for me in this life. I do these things, and I enjoy them, not because we are moral, or right—or loving souls seeking to enlighten a dark universe—but because all I feel are the Butcher's Nails hammered into my brain. I serve because of this "mutilation". Without it? Well, perhaps I might be a more moral man, like you claim to be. A virtuous man, eh? Perhaps I might ascend the steps of our father's palace and take the slaving bastard's head.“[1] How to do this in a tabletop RPG? Take my group’s current campaign. The Pathfinder Adventure Path War for the Crown is all about stopping a succession war before it starts, in one of the linchpin countries of the Inner Sea Region. Taldor is the rump state of what was once Avistan’s version of the Roman Empire, and though corrupt and doddering, it still exerts considerable influence. To the south, the Satrap of Qadira still yearns to invade the north, and his liege the Padishah of Kelesh is old and infirm. To the north, Galt is in perpetual anarchy that constantly threatens to spill over to neighboring realms. And as our GM set the campaign in the aftermath of their previous Hell’s Rebels run, Cheliax to the west is now under military occupation by a paladin crusade, and the Commonwealth of Andoran, Golarion’s only large representative democracy, is overextended between supporting the Cansellarion regime in Cheliax and the Mendevian Crusades against the demons of the Worldwound. If Taldor collapses, it’s a recipe for a multiway world war. And my character is there to prevent that, with her young daughter in tow. She claimed to be Fiorina Falco, a scion of a minor noble house in the north, in Oppara to witness the events surrounding the proposal in the Senate to allow Princess Eutropia to inherit the throne. In actual fact, she’s Sir Fiorina Mazzanti, a paladin of Shelyn serving as an Andoren foreign service operative—a Twilight Talon—with the goal of ensuring that an Andoran-friendly heir is nominated and the peace kept between Taldor and its former provinces to the west. And of course, as things go, mad old Grand Prince Stavian decided the Senate could go screw itself and brought in mercenaries to kill everyone present so he could rule as an absolute monarch, and assassins attacked the chapel where Fiorina and her young daughter Violetta had been staying, killed the priest, and kidnapped Violetta. As she said during post-session text RP: “The minute Lord Stavian tried to pervert the transition of power, he ceased to be the legitimate leader of this country. But attacking my temple and threatening my little girl made it personal.” The other PCs also had personal reasons to be involved: the arcanist, sorcerer, and bardbuckler are by-blows of various Taldan houses involved in the conflict, the cleric was trying to find his lover and his illegitimate daughter who went missing in the collapse of Cheliax—plus, he’s a Hellknight, and therefore contractually obligated to keep order wherever he goes. I’m doing similar kinds of things in the campaign I’m writing. Some of my characters are Kara, the horse peoples of central Casmaron, and the campaign is going to take place after the Padishah of Kelesh finally kicks the bucket and the succession must be decided. That’s going to draw in the tribes that some of them come from: perhaps a prince who loses a power struggle in the palace might take refuge among the horse folk. As a general rule, personal stakes do better at drawing people into a story than vague “saving the world” narratives. You don’t necessarily need to actively torture your players—Violetta turned up alive, for what it’s worth—but you ought to give them a reason beyond “there’s the bad guy, go smite him”.
