Question: Because the planes were made out of aluminum, how were they able to cause so much damage on 9/11 to steel?
Answer: Physics. This is the equation for kinetic energy: E K = m v 2 / 2 Notice this: the energy is proportional to the unity of the mass, but the square of the velocity. In other words, a heavy object moving slowly will cause some damage, but a heavy object moving fast will cause exponentially more. Always listen to Gunny Newton. United Airlines Flight 77, a Boeing 767–200ER, is estimated to have struck the North Tower traveling about 440 mph[1] at an approximate weight of 283,600 lb.[2] This is approximately a 2.5 gigajoule impact,[3] or about the detonation energy of 0.6 tons of TNT. Flight 175 struck the South Tower moving much faster, about 590 mph.[4] I haven’t been able to find an estimate of its mass on impact, so assuming the same mass gives us an impact energy of 4.5 GJ,[5] or about a ton of TNT. This is a comparison of explosions of those sizes: This is a bloody lot of energy we’re talking about. It’s more than enough to simply smash steel it strikes directly. But the buildings still stood. Causing them to collapse took something extra: the impact blasted the fire retardants off of the structural beams. Couple that with tons upon tons of blazing-hot Jet A, and what steel wasn’t blasted completely through by the impact, was weakened by the heat. Not melted, just weakened, like heating steel in a forge. You can do the same thing on a small scale with a simple propane burner. Past a certain point, the steel couldn’t hold the weight of the floors above anymore, and gave way.

Question: In Star Wars, after Niem Numb returned to piloting his own Starfighter, would he be allowed to add the DS-2 Battlestation as part of his kill talley the way Luke could paint the DS-1 Battlestation on hig fighter and Wedge Antilles got to paint both?

Name: Aaron Davis
Question: Is Tanya Dugarechaff evil?
Answer: Tanya Degureschaff is textbook Lawful Evil. Let’s get our definitions straight, first. To quote the D&D 3.5E Player’s Handbook: Lawful Evil, "Dominator" A lawful evil villain methodically takes what he wants within the limits of his code of conduct without regard for whom it hurts. He cares about tradition, loyalty, and order but not about freedom, dignity, or life. He plays by the rules but without mercy or compassion. He is comfortable in a hierarchy and would like to rule, but is willing to serve. He condemns others not according to their actions but according to race, religion, homeland, or social rank. He is loath to break laws or promises. This reluctance comes partly from his nature and partly because he depends on order to protect himself from those who oppose him on moral grounds. Some lawful evil villains have particular taboos, such as not killing in cold blood (but having underlings do it) or not letting children come to harm (if it can be helped). They imagine that these compunctions put them above unprincipled villains. Some lawful evil people and creatures commit themselves to evil with a zeal like that of a crusader committed to good. Beyond being willing to hurt others for their own ends, they take pleasure in spreading evil as an end unto itself. They may also see doing evil as part of a duty to an evil deity or master. Lawful evil is sometimes called "diabolical," because devils are the epitome of lawful evil. Lawful evil is the most dangerous alignment because it represents methodical, intentional, and frequently successful evil. [1] Now let’s talk about how this applies to Tanya. First of all, she’s a sociopath. This is abundantly demonstrated by the scene depicting her former life in Japan, and her behavior in her Imperial military career: she sees people as cogs in the machine, no more than means to an end. She can fire a man for underperformance, and then hand him a pamphlet on self-improvement, without seemingly having any comprehension of how this might be taken as adding insult to injury. She can ruthlessly order artillery strikes against columns of refugees fleeing their occupied and half-destroyed city, just because they might begrudge losing their homes and come back with guns in their hands if she doesn’t. Another fine example: the factory. Yeah, that preview image? It’s true: she wouldn’t ignore international wartime law, she’d just twist it into an unrecognizable pretzel. In this instance, she cites the laws and customs of war in the ‘verse, specifically that an attacker striking a military target surrounded by civilian infrastructure is required to issue a warning and allow time to evacuate before firing on the target. So, she does exactly that: she radios in a warning. Except she does so in her girliest possible voice, explicitly so that anybody listening thinks some kid is just prank-calling them. That way, no evacuation order goes out, and she inflicts as many casualties on the enemy as humanly possible, military and civilian alike. She didn’t violate the letter of the law. But she made the spirit of the law her bitch. See also what she does at the end of the war. With the defeated Republic’s army about to pull a Dunkirk, she tries to launch a wildcat attack to finish them off, explicitly trying to get off the ground before she can receive a ceasefire order that she full well knows is coming. Tanya Degureschaff is a bloodthirsty sociopath who delights in inflicting pain and misery, while using international law as a fig leaf to protect her own ass. She is exactly as evil as the English title of the series says she is.

Name: Aaron Davis
Question: Can an Oathbreaker Paladin in 5th Edition's Dungeon & Dragon series be lawful evil instead of chaotic evil? How would this affect the character's mechanics and story?
Answer: Can an Oathbreaker Paladin in 5th Edition's Dungeon & Dragon series be lawful evil instead of chaotic evil? Nothing in the rules forbids this. The only real restriction for the Oathbreaker subclass is that you can’t make a Good-aligned one, because the text of the fluff and class features specifically says it’s not for Good characters. The trick is the fluff is written with the assumption, carried over from earlier editions, that all characters who took the class started with Good alignment and then fell to Evil; they failed to consider the newly possible idea of a paladin who was always Evil. Mechanically, the Oathbreaker is really just 5E’s version of the Antipaladin.[1] But nothing prevents an Oathbreaker from being Lawful Evil, and frankly I think it’s an easier mental leap than (again, assuming the character started Good) going from Lawful Good all the way to Chaotic Evil. In fact, we have a preexisting example (sort of) in canon. This is Scyllua Darkhope, a champion of Bane, god of tyranny in the Forgotten Realms setting. In her backstory she was a paladin of Tyr, god of justice, but fell to evil. Where once she fought to preserve law and justice for the benefit of all Faerûn, now she fights to put the iron boot of the Zhentarim onto the necks of everyone in Faerûn. In Third Edition, she was statted as a Lawful Evil Blackguard—the evil equivalent of a paladin in that edition (in fact, they were allowed to treat preexisting paladin levels as levels of Blackguard). The equivalence between a 3E Blackguard and a 5E Oathbreaker Paladin is basically a 1:1 conversion. How would this affect the character's mechanics and story? Mechanically it makes no difference at all. None of the class features are dependent on the Law-Chaos axis of the alignment grid. Story-wise, you have to make a determination of your character’s code. At its most basic, that’s all Lawful alignment means: they have a clear personal code, whether externally imposed or internally invented, and use that to determine their course of action and how to interact with others. Frequently, a Lawful Evil character is much more interested in the letter of the law than the spirit of the law. Devils, Lawful Evil outsiders, are particularly known for their insanely verbose contracts that are written to ensure they always come out ahead on the deal (and, being immortal, they can afford to wait). A Lawful Evil paladin tied to one of the gods of the Nine Hells might follow suit. For example, they might assiduously adhere to the laws and customs of war… and bend and reinterpret them as far as humanly possible for their own benefit. Case in point: In this scene from The Saga of Tanya the Evil, international law requires a military force striking a legitimate military target surrounded by civilian housing and infrastructure to issue a warning and allow time to evacuate before opening fire. So Tanya Degureschaff does exactly that. Except she deliberately gives the warning in her girliest possible voice so that the workers at the factory think some kid is prank-calling them and don’t evacuate, meaning that she inflicts as many casualties on the enemy country as she possibly can, military and civilian alike, without technically breaking the laws of war. There's similar scenes later where she twists the laws of war to justify shelling refugees, and then tries to launch a wildcat attack against a retreating army when it pulls a Dunkirk, and specifically tries to get it off the ground before she receives official ceasefire orders that she full well knows are coming. That's textbook Lawful Evil.

Question: What book series should I read? I'm 15 years old and I’ve read the Harry Potter books, the Narnia books, both Percy Jackson series, and the Saga of Darren Shan. I tried reading Game Of Thrones but I'm up to date with the show.
Answer: Since you bring up Harry Potter, I suggest Reign of the Seven Spellblades by Bokuto Uno. It’s a Japanese YA dark fantasy novel series heavily inspired by the Potterverse but still plenty distinct. The novels and the manga adaptation by Sakae Esuno (creator of Future Diary) are available in English from Yen Press, and an anime adapting the first three volumes aired in summer and fall 2023. Much like Harry Potter, Nanatsuma (the contraction of its Japanese title Nanatsu no Maken ga Shihai Suru) follows six freshman students at an elite magical boarding school in a world ruled by mages. When a troll goes berserk during the opening ceremonies and nearly tramples the animal-loving Katie Aalto, all-rounder Oliver Horn (the main protagonist), hotheaded farm boy Guy Greenwood, nonmagical-born bookworm Pete Reston, and aristocrat Chela McFarlane jump in to rescue her—and are joined by an ex-samurai from the far eastern land of Yamatsu, Nanao Hibiya, who quickly connects on a spiritual level with Oliver. (Art by novel illustrator Miyuki Ruria. Clockwise from right, Oliver Horn, Nanao Hibiya, Katie Aalto, Guy Greenwood, Pete Reston, and Michela “Chela” McFarlane.) The first part of the series has a lot of similarities to Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone, with the A-plot being an investigation of a string of unusual events at the school starting with the troll attack, but there are some major differences. Kimberly Magic Academy is a school about combat, where an order of battlemages called the Gnostic Hunters regularly recruits graduates. Dueling is considered the accepted way to settle disputes, and there are classes on swordplay and both unofficial and official tournaments for individuals and teams. Mages traditionally carry short swords, “athames”, in addition to wands, which serve as both magic foci and sidearms. Second, a lot of the flaws people often complain about with the Wizarding World are taken and turned into deliberate features of a dystopia: the core conflict of the series is much more “Man versus Society” than “Man versus Man”. Mages as a whole are obsessed to an often unhealthy degree with pushing the boundaries of magic, and as a direct consequence this world sucks to live in almost as badly for mages as it does for nonmagicals and demihumans. Some want this to change, but many don’t: Headmistress Esmeralda practically brags in her opening address to the freshman class that one in five of them will be dead, “consumed by the spell”, before their seven-year course of study is complete. So rather than pit the protagonists against wizard neo-Nazis attacking from outside, the enemies are all right there in the school: part and parcel of the fucked-up system everyone’s trapped in, not malcontents trying to overthrow a merely flawed world from outside. Mage children are victimized in traumatic generational cycles by mage families trying to get ahead, nonmagicals are second-class citizens at best, and intelligent nonhumans are third-class if they’re lucky: one of the professors laments the fact she’s not allowed to snack on centaur livers anymore because the reformists are starting to actually make forward progress. And Oliver Horn? Well, best not spoil that… It’s also much more open than Harry Potter about the fact that these are teenagers (the admission age to Kimberly is 15, not 10), so obviously they’re going to be interested in sex. The adaptations tone this down, but the original novels regularly touch on romantic complications, contraception and teen pregnancy, queer issues (by my count, eleven named characters so far are LGBT+ in some respect including a main cast member, and there’s a student club for sex-related magical traits that acts as the in-universe equivalent of a queer student union), and consent—or more often the lack thereof. Sex is just as frequently weaponized by mages as everything else: mages often practice selective breeding on themselves to produce stronger children, and Ophelia Salvadori’s history of sex abuse is extremely important to volume 3 (episodes 12–15 of the anime). As a recovering Potterhead, I found this series enchanting: it deals directly with a lot of my current complaints about the series while still being similar enough to be nostalgic, the characters react realistically to their troubles and to their various conflicting priorities, and I’m a sucker for the slow-burn romance between Oliver and Nanao, which feels much more natural than what we often get in YA literature.

Question: What seemingly useless college degree is actually a dark horse in the job market?
Answer: All of them. That is to say: There’s no such thing as a “useless” degree. There’s just useless university Career Services desks. I’m currently attending North Carolina A&T State University for a B.S. in Electrical Engineering. I started during the pandemic so we were remote for the first couple of years, but when they started doing in-person classes again, something really stuck out to me compared to my previous college experience (Central Carolina Community College, Durham Tech, and UNC Greensboro). This school goes ham on connecting students with employers. There’s at least two career fairs every semester (one each for STEM and humanities majors), and every student gets email blasts several times a week about recruiting events both online and in-person. Seriously, I can get a free lunch roughly once a week just by showing up for a company tech talk in McNair or the Student Union. And when I go to a tech talk, the school’s corporate relations officer insists that you give your name, year, and major before you ask a question, so that the host actually remembers which kid it was who asked a bright question about upcoming chip technologies or what-have-you. None of the three previous universities I’ve attended worked this hard. My AAS at Durham Tech had a co-op as a graduation requirement, but I had no idea where to even start looking for that and ended up spending a miserable semester shadowing the facility services electrician when I wasn’t in class. The result was that I spent the better part of five years either unemployed or bouncing from temp agency to temp agency, because nobody taught me how to market myself or conduct myself on the job and, being autistic, it’s not something that I just naturally know how to do. Nor do a lot of the folks who come to this school: NC A&T is a Historically Black College and University (HBCU), meaning a higher-than-average proportion of students who are the first in their families to try at higher education, and therefore inherit little to no professional network or support structure. The school has to give them a leg up just to get them onto the bottom rung of the career ladder. Now, I may be an engineering student, but one of the things I’ve learned here is that soft skills are just as important as STEM academics, and those skills exist across all majors. If you did a class project? That shows you can do research, write reports, meet deadlines. Maybe you have project management experience if you had to take charge when a group member dropped the class. Ever have to go ask a professor for an extension on a homework? That’s use of communication skills: you had to have the courage and humility to ask for help, and you had to explain your needs to somebody who probably didn’t know you from Adam before. Where other universities are falling down is not that they’re offering the wrong degrees, it’s that they’re not actively teaching students how to talk to employers and translate their skills into things employers are looking for. They default to expecting students who are probably out of the house for the first time in their entire lives to automatically know that you find proper jobs by networking, not listing off your skills on a resume. They expect you to just know how to be an adult in the workforce, and that simply isn’t a realistic expectation.

Question: Which actors from war movies have had actual combat experience in the wars depicted?
Answer: Sir Christopher Lee. Known especially frequently playing villains in speculative fiction, including Dracula, Saruman, and Count Dooku, Sir Christopher Lee first served in a British volunteer unit in Finland during the Winter War, then joined the Royal Air Force in 1941. Question: What is the behavior of female praying mantises after mating? Do they always eat their mates or is it a rare occurrence?
Answer: Rare in the wild, common in captivity. Contrary to popular belief, post-coital cannibalism is actually the least-likely scenario among mantises. As a rule, they have no qualms about eating each other, but when one mantis eats another, it’s usually just because they’re hungry and the victim was the closest prey available. And adult female mantises tend to be bigger than males, so it’s usually them eating the male rather than the other way around. The tendency towards sexual cannibalism was first noticed in human captivity, which disrupts the normal mating behavior in a lot of ways: among other things, the female may not have been fed properly by the human keepers, or the male may have been unable to get away in time. In the wild, if a female kills a male, they were usually just hungrier than they were horny, or it was a—admittedly excessive—way of rejecting the suitor. And it usually happens before intercourse, not after: a male that succeeds in doing the deed will more likely than not survive.

Question: Can the old "THAC0" system be incorporated into the new "Armor Class" system in 5e Dungeons and Dragons without creating overly complex or confusing house rules?
Answer: No point. “THAC0″ is an abbreviation meaning “to hit AC 0”. It literally describes what you need to roll in order to hit a target's Armor Class, it just does it in a more opaque manner than saying “roll d20+modifiers and meet or beat this number”. THAC0 is literally the same mechanic as an attack roll but with extra steps. Gygax just had an unnecessary fetish for charts: in 3+ Edition, the rulebook just tells you what the formula is that was used to calculate those charts.

Name: Aaron Davis
Question: What rules, references, or books do you still use from past editions of gaming rules like D&D or Pathfinder? What would you recommend to others even though they’re no longer in wide use?
Answer: One of the nice things about running Pathfinder First Edition is that, in addition to the wide selection of Paizo's own books to draw from, you can pull in the even bigger selection of D&D Third and 3.5 Edition books with very little statblock rewriting. There’s a few specific 3.5E books that I’ve dug out of my collection for the needs of my specific campaign (Lost Empires of Faerûn for one[1]), but if you want recommendations of a few that are more broadly usable, then let’s start with The Draconomicon. This is one of the biggest books that Wizards ever printed during Third Edition. Seriously, it’s thicc. This is a setting-agnostic book that contains everything you could ever possibly want to know about the second half of the name “Dungeons & Dragons” and then some: not just statblocks and quick blurbs, but extended essays on dragons’ biology, life cycles, mating and childrearing habits, what individual species like and don’t like, how they think, how they interact, you name it. Even if you never roll a single d20 with any of the statblocks in this book,* the information in it is indispensable for running dragon-related adventures. * Some of which are actually really cool: there’s a couple of prestige classes for dragons (one good, one evil) that let you give a level of a divine spellcasting class to a dragon and then treat the dragon’s effective levels of sorcerer from its age as extra levels of the divine class instead. Second, The Book of Exalted Deeds and The Book of Vile Darkness. These two books together (as well as their Forgotten Realms-specific counterparts Champions of Valor and Champions of Ruin) contain some of the better musings on the fundamental nature of the forces of Good and Evil, and what it means to be good or evil in the context of D&D. For example, it makes the argument that a truly Good character needs to be actively trying to do good: a character who merely talks about all the evil things they haven’t done is Neutral at best. They also explicitly point out that a paladin is supposed to default to the Good over the Law if they’re caught in a situation where the two are in conflict. There are admittedly a few things in them that didn’t age well (The Book of Vile Darkness has a bit of a hard-on for BDSM, and The Book of Exalted Deeds has “they’re mind-control drugs BUT THEY’RE TOTALLY GOOD, OKAY?!”), but overall they still mostly hold up. Third, Faiths of Eberron. Most Dungeons & Dragons settings have a very simplistic view of religion, in that there is only one of them: polytheism. Worshiping one god versus worshiping another god is a matter of personal preference: you still fundamentally accept that all the gods are real, you just have one or more in particular that you like better than the others. The Eberron setting, which was first officially published during 3.5E, is very different. Multiple entirely separate and mutually contradictory religions exist, much like in the real world where the Abrahamic faiths (which all claim to worship the same god, even if they claim the other two are doing it wrong) exist alongside Hinduism and Shintoism, neopagan faiths like Wicca and Asatru, and many still-extant indigenous faiths. Similarly in Eberron, the basic D&D polytheist faith of the Sovereign Host and Dark Six exists alongside the henotheistic Silver Flame faith, the Blood of Vol mystery cult which claims the only divinity exists within mankind itself, the fully atheistic quori Paths, and the ancestor worship of the isle of Aerenal. As a consequence of which, this book contains some of the better philosophical takes on the fundamental nature of religion—what it actually means to be a religious person beyond treating your divine patron as a vending machine for cool powers—that Wizards ever published. Understanding how religion works in your world is, I think, a very important worldbuilding concern: if a priest has real, measurable power—as indeed they do in most D&D worlds—then where does that power come from? And can that power be removed if you displease your patron? If you talk to God, does God talk back? Or are priests really just a weird kind of wizard and the gods aren’t actually real?

Name: Aaron Davis
Question: If the Yuuzhan Vong invaded during the rise of the Empire, would Darth Vader, Emperor Palpatine and the Inquisitors be able to stop them or would they all be defeated easily?
Answer: There’s actually two different questions here: Would the Empire at its height have beaten the Yuuzhan Vong? Yes, probably. After all, the New Republic canonically managed it eventually. Would it have been because of Emperor Palpatine and his various darksider hangers-on? No, it wouldn’t have. This is why the Empire beats the Yuuzhan Vong: It has a functioning combined-arms military. Yuuzhan Vong biotechnology, as it turns out, isn’t actually any better than the technology of the Galaxy Far, Far Away, it’s just different. In some cases it’s actually worse: The strength of the Empire in this scenario is that, coming off of the Clone Wars and the reoccupation of the former Confederacy of Independent Systems, it has a veteran, battle-hardened army and navy that is used to fighting in set-piece battles. They had trouble fighting the Rebellion because, up until Yavin 4, the Rebels refused to stand and fight: like any good guerrilla army, they attacked where the regular military wasn’t. The Yuuzhan Vong don’t do this. They fight conventional-style warfare, meeting force with force. The New Republic brings up a star destroyer or Mon Cal cruiser, the Vong bring up a matalok or miid ro’ik. This is the kind of war that the Empire is used to fighting. Couple that with interior lines of supply, against an enemy whose ships are literally starting to die of old age from being in intergalactic space for too long, and a far more intrusive state security apparatus than the New Republic ever had—because it actually believed civil liberties were a thing citizens deserved to have—and you’ve got the recipe for the war ending with a whole lot of really ugly slaves getting sold to the Hutts to recoup the operating budget. Also you probably end up with a stronger and more united Empire, since Palpatine is hardly the kind of guy to let a perfectly good crisis go to waste, and he didn’t even have to manufacture it this time. The presence or absence of Force-users is basically irrelevant, because there are never enough of them to matter overmuch in a conventional war, especially against an enemy that the Force doesn't directly work on. In the canon Yuuzhan Vong War, the New Jedi Order essentially only played special forces and intelligence roles.

Question: In Dungeons and Dragons, what were the problems caused by the spell plague?
Answer: None at all. There was no Spellplague in the world of Greyhawk. Nor was there a Spellplague in Eberron. Nor Dark Sun. Nor Nentir Vale. Not even Ravenloft. And forget Golarion, that’s a whole other company. What I’m getting at is that you need to separate the Dungeons & Dragons game from the Forgotten Realms campaign setting. The Spellplague was a specific feature of the Forgotten Realms setting under the Fourth Edition rules that happened because, for whatever reason, Ed Greenwood decided he needed to have in-universe justifications for the rule changes between game editions, and his go-to reason is “somebody killed the goddess of magic again”. None of the other major official campaign settings do anything like this: they just continue the old stories under the new rules. So your question is based on an incorrect premise.

Name: Aaron Davis
Question: Why didn’t World War 1’s Christmas truce of 1914 happen in any other year of the war?
Answer: Well, first of all, the Christmas Truce wasn't a widespread thing. It happened in some places, but other parts of the front were just as active as ever on Christmas. The truces were an informal thing that just happened: a bunch of conscripts on both sides just decided, fuck this, I'm cold and miserable and I'm not fighting on Christmas, and then they started singing carols to themselves, and then recognized some of what their opposite numbers were singing and joined in. Second, the brass and the politicians got tremendously pissed off that the enlisted men and junior officers would rather sing Christmas carols and play football than fight each other. Units that had taken part in the truce were reassigned, and their officers threatened with court-martial, because how dare they undermine a stupid, pointless war they had no actual stake in? Then, by the time next Christmas rolled around, the bloodshed had become too set in stone to overcome. There was an attempt on the Eastern Front to organize an Easter truce in 1915, but because the Russian Empire still used the Julian calendar, their date for Easter was two weeks off from the German date, and the soldiers who tried to celebrate Easter with their enemy were all taken prisoner.

Name: Aaron Davis
Question: How many times have imperial troopers actually hit someone? I just saw Mandalorian, s03e04 The foundling, and a Jedi was hit, and I was shocked.
Answer: What you're talking about is a basic fact of fiction. You're telling a story, and you need to have characters. It gets labeled “plot armor” if you do it badly, but it comes back to this basic fact: If the bad guys ever actually hit anyone important, the movie would be over. In other words you can't kill off important characters unless it is narratively appropriate for them to die. Not even the likes of George R.R. Martin is going to have an important nobleman die of a random wound from some nobody, the way Karl XII of Sweden just randomly got hit by a piece of grapeshot. No, if he's going to kill them off, he's going to save it for something dramatic like a beheading or the Red Wedding. The trick is to make it non-obvious that you're protecting those characters. Take, as an example, the opening scene of A New Hope. What the stormtroopers in the opening scene are doing is a breach-and-clear, one of the most dangerous operations that exists in all of warfare. Your enemy knows where you're coming from (note the Alderaanians preparing a position on the interior side), and the doorway restricts the amount of men and firepower that you can put through. It is for this reason that in medieval siege warfare, the first units through a breach were nicknamed “forlorn hope”: because they were basically dead men walking. This is why hand grenades were invented. Now, notice how many casualties the stormtroopers suffer before the Alderaanians rout: a whopping two. And granted, this is the elite 501st we're dealing with, but the rest of the Stormtrooper Corps aren't much worse. But then notice that R2-D2 and C-3PO are able to just waltz through the crossfire and not take a hit. They're important characters. George Lucas can't kill them off because he's using them to tell the story: in fact, in the oldest version of his story, Artoo was the narrator. Now notice what happened when Lucas's student Dave Filoni wrote a battle scene in The Book of Boba Fett. The protagonists get hit by far lower-quality mooks than the Empire's best all the time. But they're both wearing full suits of beskar'gam. They can take a blaster hit or three. Also, people who haven't handled firearms just generally underestimate how hard it is to actually hit a target with them. It's far from impossible but it's a lot harder than Hollywood makes it look—because, as previously mentioned, Hollywood is telling a story. It's estimated that 90-something percent of shots fired in real battles hit nothing important at all.

Question: If two Galaxy Class starships separated but during battle one ship loses the saucer section, the other loses the stardrive, and the remains of the two ships connect, which captain of those sections have full command of this unified vessel?
Answer: As several answers including Murphy Barrett’s have noted, in the real world, the determining factors for which officer is in command are as follows, in descending order of priority: However, Starfleet is not the US Navy. They have their own rules, which we are introduced to on a number of occasions. First of all, scratch Item #3. According to Star Trek: The Next Generation, Starfleet allows any officer, regardless of specialty, to be certified to command a “starship”—Starfleet’s equivalent terminology for a “combatant ship”—as long as they pass something called the “Bridge Officer’s Test”. This includes tests of both knowledge and command ability: in TNG: “Thine Own Self”, we’re shown Commander Troi attempting the test, and being required to (in a simulation) knowingly send Lieutenant Commander La Forge to his death in order to save the ship. Not exactly what she thought she was signing up for. Second, we can scratch Item #4. According to Star Trek: Voyager, rather than using time-in-grade, Starfleet’s rule is apparently whose ship is more badass. This is according to “Equinox”, where the cruiser-weight USS Voyager runs across the eponymous USS Equinox, a Nova-class planetary survey ship that’s supposed to be running around behind the big exploration ships doing deeper study of what they find (rather like USS Cerritos in Lower Decks). So, by the regs, Janeway wins that contest. This, I think, is the key rule. Most of a Galaxy-class starship’s fighting power is housed in the stardrive section: the stardrive hosts the warp core, both torpedo launchers, and nine out of eleven phaser arrays. Meanwhile the saucer only has two phaser arrays and can’t even independently travel at warp. Therefore, in a theoretical situation where you had two ranked Captains (OF-6), each of them in command of a Galaxy-class starship that underwent saucer separation and had the other half rendered inoperable, the tipping point is that the stardrive is the more powerful combatant than the saucer, so the Captain with a stardrive takes priority over the Captain with a saucer. It bears mentioning, however, that this is not really how saucer separation is meant to be used. The original idea behind saucer separation is that the saucer serves as an escape ship for the nonessential crew and civilians in combat situations. They just never really used this idea after “Encounter at Farpoint” because the saucer separation sequence took too long to use every week, and the writers decided in hindsight that putting children on a ship that was being sent into mortal danger every week was kind of a rotten idea. Separating the saucer as a combat tactic a la “The Best of Both Worlds, Part II” was an improvisation and very much not what this ability of the GCS was meant for.

Question: Our class is learning imaginary numbers. My teacher firmly believes that they aren't really part of math, and aren't actual numbers. Could I show otherwise with just concepts from Algebra 1 and below?
Answer: Afraid not. Imaginary numbers are a real part of math and are actually extremely useful, but you won't be dealing with them on any regular basis unless you decide to major in a STEM field in university. That's where you start to get real-world use cases for them. I'll give you an example. This is the kind of thing I’m working towards doing for a living as an electrical engineer. I made this circuit diagram using a free applet. It takes a 120V 60 Hz alternating current input—exactly what comes out of standard a wall outlet in the United States—and transmits it from the generating station to a mixed load, representing, for example, a house. (I was originally going to include a step-down transformer, too, but couldn't remember the math offhand.) Now, how would you calculate the total impedance—simply put how hard the loads push back against the electricity—of this device? If you said “you use imaginary numbers”, have a cookie. The mixed load at the end has resistive, capacitive, and inductive components. Admittedly pretty much everything does, but with a simple resistive load such as an incandescent light bulb, the capacitance and inductance are so small they’re not worth discussing. In this case however, we have two defined non-resistive impedances, which are defined as follows: ω, i.e. a lowercase Greek letter omega, is simply the “angular frequency”. We calculate this by taking our power source’s frequency of 60Hz (60 complete up-down cycles per second) and multiplying it by 2π. ω = 2 π f = 120 π r a d / s From here it’s basic circuit analysis. We can convert this into what’s called the phase angle, which describes the spacing in time between the voltage and current waveforms. As shown, a strongly inductive load will cause the current to lag behind the voltage, whereas a strongly capacitive load will cause the current to lead the voltage. Calculating this angle from our imaginary domain impedance is very easy: So our angular impedance is 55.32∠-74.93° kΩ. This tells us we have a significantly capacitive load, causing a leading power factor. This is a bad thing: among other effects, it can potentially damage the generator. So this tells us we need to install additional inductive loads nearby to raise the power factor,[1] something like this: This is not the only place you’ll use imaginary numbers in science, but it’s a relatively easy example (one that doesn't involve differential equations, which you need calculus to even begin to wrap your head around). Imaginary numbers show up a lot in situations where you have oscillations or vibrations: alternating current is one example, the swaying of trees or tall buildings is another.

Question: Why is it a stereotype that Jewish business people are shrewd when most business men are, especially Jewish ones that I’ve met?
Answer: This one goes back a long, long, time. Essentially what happened was, when the Roman Catholic Church was still dominant in Europe in the Middle Ages, most laws were written largely in accordance with Catholic doctrine. This included bans on “usury”—charging excessive interest on a loan, corresponding to a couple dozen Bible verses in both Testaments.[1] At the same time, the Jewish diaspora in Europe was banned from pursuing most trades because they weren’t Christian, so the tradesmens’ guilds kept them out. So they got pushed into being merchants or bankers because the Christians by and large weren’t doing those businesses because the Church said it was wrong to. And there we get a funny twist. Because the first “Christians” were in fact Jews, the Tanakh, the Bible used in Judaism, is essentially the same document as the Christian Bible’s Old Testament (plus or minus the odd translation error or edit).[2] So it has the same prohibitions on usury as the Christian Bible: you’re not allowed to charge excessive interest to a poor person or to one of your own people, but not, key point, to foreigners. And the Christians weren’t exactly treating the European Jews as part of their own people, so the Jews responded accordingly and considered them “foreigners” to whom they could charge greater interest. Add to this that Judaism more generally encourages education and debate to a much greater degree than Christianity does, and you get Jewish businesspeople being better-educated on average than their Christian counterparts, and therefore better at driving a bargain. So in other words, the stereotype of the “shrewd” or “greedy” Jew is a complete own-goal by medieval anti-Semites.

Question: Why are only the men of Arnor (not of Gondor) called "Dunedain" if the name means "Man/Men of the West"?

These states were all shattered during a series of wars with the nation of Angmar (as in “the Witch-King of”), so all that’s left of them is the Rangers of the North. The Dúnedain of Gondor are traditionally called the “Men of the South”. Their state was a vassal of Arnor during the War of the Last Alliance but became independent following the death of King Isildur, and is still standing. They also heavily interbred with the Men of neighboring Rhovanion, so they have comparatively less Númenórean ancestry than the Rangers. They’re not usually called Dúnedain simply because they still have a nation-state and so are called Men of Gondor instead, so in the Third Age “Dúnedain” is usually used to refer to the Rangers. Question: What is the difference between anachronism and time jumping (flashback and flashforward) in literature?
Answer: Anachronism is a factual error in the portrayal of a time period. What you’re calling “time jumping” is simply showing the same work at different in-universe times. I’m going to show you a film with examples of both. The excellent film A Knight's Tale is deliberately and gleefully anachronistic in many respects. It's a modern-style sports movie with a classic rock soundtrack and a romantic comedy subplot… that happens to be set in late 14th century France during the Hundred Years’ War, and the sport is jousting. The film is loosely based on the first story from Geoffrey Chaucer’s anthology The Canterbury Tales, depicting an English yeoman, William Thatcher (played by the late Heath Ledger), trying to rise above his common roots and become a knight. To that end, he squires for a poor knight named Sir Ector for almost nine years, then Sir Ector suddenly dies of a heart attack while trying to take a crap between bouts. William and his fellow servants Roland (Mark Addy) and Wat (Alan Tudyk), penniless and starving, dress William in Ector’s armor and have him finish the joust so they can eat and get home on the prize money. And they come on to the tournament pitch to the tune of “We Will Rock You” by Queen, released in 1977. The sequence was originally filmed as a joke, but they decided it was so awesome afterwards that they left it in the final cut of the film. The justification they gave for using a classic rock soundtrack in a film about jousting was to show the audience that medieval people thought their music was just as cool as we think ours is. But this is far from the only anachronism in the film: for example, the majority of the clothing worn by William’s love interest Lady Jocelyn (Shannyn Sossamon) is completely inaccurate to how a typical 14th century Anglo-French noblewoman would have dressed. Yeah, showing her cleavage under sheer gauze to her navel? Not a thing. You’re more likely to get an off-the-shoulder button-front dress like this. Later in the film, we get a couple of flashbacks, for example this one depicting William’s father John taking him across the English Channel to meet Sir Ector for the first time.

Question: Pathfinder 1st Edition: I'm a RL martial artist raised on '70s HK fantasy/period Kung Fu flicks. How do I create a playable Monk character who isn't a trope?
Answer: You can't. But you don't actually want to: tropes are not bad things. Tropes are tools. Now, if you’re looking for advice on a non-stereotypical monk or monk-like character, then let’s go to some other potential inspirations. And I’m glad you said you were working with Pathfinder, because that’s my primary system. If you really want to get non-stereotypical, you might want to start from your basics: the build design. Have a look at the list of Monk archetypes and find something interesting. First of all, an actual Pathfinder Monk character: Lann, from the Wrath of the Righteous video game adaptation. Lann is a mongrelman who grew up in the caverns and catacombs beneath the city of Kenabres on the edge of the Worldwound. He’s descended from early crusaders whose bodies were mutated by exposure to the energies of the Worldwound, and joins the PC when they fall into a chasm opened through the center of Kenabres when the demon lord Deskari attacks the city. As a person, he’s a fairly easygoing joker, but he cares deeply about protecting his tribe. That’s his “law”. Lann can fight hand-to-hand, but he uses the Zen Archer archetype. This switches out most of the list of Monk bonus feats with ranged weapon feats, and allows monks to use their Flurry of Blows feature with bow attacks. Another interesting archetype is the Menhir Guardian. This gives the monk some features of Shifters. Quoth Ultimate Wilderness, “Menhir guardians are ascetic protectors of sacred druidic sites, less concerned with structure and maintaining internal order than they are with preserving the natural balance of the world.” So this could perhaps be a Monk interested in ending exploitation of wild spaces, which gives you and your GM an opening to create conflict between yourself and the Powers That Be. Now let’s move away from the pure Monk to adjacent classes. Say hello to Lesedi Ingwe, from the light novel series Reign of the Seven Spellblades by Bokuto Uno. She’s a mage in a wizarding school series. Mages in this series normally carry short swords called athames, which are used as both a magic focus and a sidearm for close combat. Lesedi doesn’t. She instead prefers magic-enhanced kickboxing. This is considered extremely unorthodox, but mages in the series generally prioritize strength and power over all else, so she shuts people up herself. I designed a version of her as a premade for use in convention one-shots. I made her a Magus, using the Esoteric archetype, which is a hybridization of Magus and Monk: she gets Improved Unarmed Strike for free and treats her Magus levels as Monk levels for the purposes of unarmed strike damage, as well as letting her treat her arcane pool as a ki pool for the purposes of feat and ability requirements. Furthermore, for her first magus arcana, I gave her Flamboyant Arcana, which allows her to use the Derring-Do and Opportune Parry and Riposte swashbuckler deeds. So she can literally punch away incoming sword blows and counterattack. There’s a similar archetype for paladins, the Iroran Paladin, which allows a paladin worshiping the Lost Omens monk god Irori to fight unarmed like a monk.

Question: In Star Wars, if someone was cut off from the Force, like for example the Yuuzhan Vong, does it also mean that Force powers like Force Push or choke did not work on them or affect them at all? Or does it sork differently?
Answer: This was something that The New Jedi Order never actually properly settled: the dozen or so authors who worked on the series contradicted each other multiple times. The series was reasonably consistent that mind-related Force powers (illusions, compulsions, telepathy) absolutely did not work on the Yuuzhan Vong, nor did precognition. However, physical powers were portrayed inconsistently. Some authors wrote that you couldn't do anything directly to any Vong creation at all, but then somebody else would write a Jedi unmasking Nom Anor in one of his various guises by hitting the “off switch” on his ooglith masquer with telekinesis. Many books also showed Jedi affecting Vong indirectly: in other words, you couldn't pick a Vong up and throw them, but Streen could manipulate the air around them and blow them down. Also, in Star By Star, the Jedi strike team encounters some dark Jedi on Myrkr, and it turns out that Force lightning works just fine. Jedi also found that the fact they couldn't sense a Vong through the Force actually made their infiltrators easier to spot: the absence in Force perception of a person they could physically see and hear was a giveaway. And Jacen and Anakin Solo both discovered through experiments with a lambent (a living crystal used by Vong as illumination, which Anakin used to replace his lightsaber's focusing crystal after it was damaged when the Vong attacked Yavin 4) that they could alter their perception to pick the Vong up, at the cost of temporarily losing access to their normal perception: they had to switch back and forth.

Answer: Jim Trotter III. Jim Trotter (played by Lane Smith) is the prosecutor for the State of Alabama in the 1992 legal comedy My Cousin Vinny. Question: What is an example of divergent or convergent evolution that has occurred in humans since our divergence from chimps?
Answer: Here’s a good example of convergent evolution in humans: not in our biology, but in culture. The ancient Romans highly prized a condiment called garum. It was made by packing lots of small fish like herring or anchovies in salt and letting them ferment. This created a sauce that was packed with monosodium glutamate (MSG). Trading in garum was immensely profitable: the Romans couldn’t get enough of it. Garum largely fell out of favor in Europe after the fall of the Roman Empire. However, halfway across the globe in southeast Asia, the same basic process is still used today. We call it “fish sauce” (nam pla in Thai). The same basic idea occurred independently in two macrocultures thousands of miles apart that never heard of each other. That’s convergent cultural evolution.

Question: Why are dark-type Pokemon immune to psychic-type moves? Is it because of satanophobia, fear of malevolent creatures, or other reasons?
Answer: Game balance. I'm old enough to remember the Gen I games. Psychic-type Pokémon were basically completely broken in the type system: their Special stat was invariably through the roof so they were good on attack and defense, nothing but another Psychic-type was resistant to them, and they had no meaningful weaknesses. They were supposed to be weak to Bug and Ghost-type attacks, but there were about two extremely sucky Bug-type attacks and most of the Pokémon that could use them were weak to Psychic themselves, and because of a database error (corrected in Yellow Version), Psychic-types were instead immune to Ghost-type attacks. The introduction of Dark and Steel types in Gen II was completely about balancing Psychic properly. Steel is resistant, Dark is immune and Psychic is weak to it, and the common Normal-type move Bite was made a Dark-type move. If you want an in-universe explanation, Dark-type moves have a bit of a theme: fighting dirty. Question: Is Boba Fett a true Mandalorian?
Answer: No, because he himself says in The Mandalorian that he isn’t. Canon has gone back and forth on this repeatedly. Originally, Boba Fett was stated in Alan Dean Foster’s novelization of The Empire Strikes Back to wear armor made to a Mandalorian pattern. George Lucas always insisted this was meant to be literally true: the Fetts were not themselves culturally or ethnically Mandalorian, they just used Mandalorian-style gear. All we knew about the Mandalorians at this time was that they were an ancient race of evildoers who hunted Jedi. However, fanon tended to ignore this because Boba Fett was cool-looking, and until the 1990s he was basically the only example of anything resembling a Mandalorian that we had. The EU at this time, in particular a trilogy of short stories by Daniel Keys Moran, declared that he had once been a man named Jaster Mereel, a Mandalorian Journeyman Protector, who had taken the new identity Boba Fett after escaping imprisonment for murdering another Journeyman Protector. The Mandalorians began to be expanded with the Tales of the Jedi comic book series and Knights of the Old Republic—for a fuller explanation, see Eric Lowe’s essay on the subject—and even after Attack of the Clones came out and overrode the prior Legends explanation of his background, Boba Fett got his own junior novel series that begins shortly before Attack of the Clones and follows him trying to recover his father’s money and learning to be a bounty hunter. The final word on the subject is that Jango Fett was born on Mandalore and raised as a Mandalorian Foundling, so he is an ethnic Mandalorian. Question: How would you recreate Goblin Slayer in DnD?
Answer: Standard D&D isn’t my primary rule system: I prefer Pathfinder First Edition. The Goblin Slayer is, of course, a purist and specialist at battling goblins. He studies them extensively and is also skilled at adapting to non-goblin foes such as ogres. Additionally, he displays great wisdom in his pragmatic approach to battle: goblins fight dirty, but he fights dirtier. He ignores any notion of heroism and focuses on killing the enemy as efficiently and safely as possible. As the narrator of the original novels puts it, “He does not roll the dice.” First the obvious: he’s human, Ranger is the obvious class given the Favored Enemy feature, and he uses a sword-and-board combat style. Rangers can wear up to medium armor, which strikes the balance that the Goblin Slayer likes to have between protection and mobility. He is a capable archer but prefers close combat. As a rule, he prefers short, broad-bladed swords so that they’re less likely to accidentally get caught on the walls, and he uses his shield as a weapon, not just a defense. The obvious proxy for this in the Pathfinder armory is the gladius, the classic Roman infantry sword (one assumes Taldan origin in the Golarion setting). It has the same stats as the short sword but can inflict slashing damage as well as piercing, and it’s a light weapon so it can be used as the offhand weapon next to a heavy shield with the Two-Weapon Fighting feat. Image credit: Cold Steel Knives[1] Based on his specialty in rooting out, invading, and destroying goblin dens, as well as his habit of dousing himself with goblin gore to hide his scent, we’ll take the Dungeon Rover and Infiltrator archetypes. This trades away some of the Ranger’s capabilities in open country in exchange for increased facility with traps and underground work, as well as letting him take on some of his favored enemies’ abilities, like darkvision. He displays great combat skills; however, his people skills are quite lacking and he doesn’t have a lot of book learning. Given an elite stat array and humans’ built-in +2 to any stat, we’ll start with base stats of 18 Str, 13 Dex, 12 Con, 10 Int, 16 Wis, 8 Cha. For traits as a player character, we’ll take Ambush Training, Bred for War, then the Stigmatized drawback to reflect his social withdrawal, and that lets us buy a third trait, Knowing the Enemy. Lawful Neutral seems appropriate for alignment: killing goblins is his whole life, and he has a ton of rules about it. And now we’ll build him to 5th level. Rangers get 6 + Int mod skill ranks per level; humans get an extra skill point per level and an extra 1st-level feat. Prepared spells: detect snares and pits, lead blades.

Question: How would someone create a successful international bank in the DnD universe? What challenges would owners face vs. won’t face in our world?
Answer: This is actually a really interesting worldbuilding question. There’s a very good anime called Spice & Wolf, originally a novel series by Isuna Hasekura, that covers a lot of this. It’s very well-researched and instructive on the topic, but it’s all pretty basic macroeconomics. The concept of “credit” has existed for a very long time. Since long before the invention of electronic funds transfers, banks and merchant guilds would make loans to people on the trust that they would get paid back and possibly make a profit on the loan. People could also carry letters of credit, essentially promises between institutions that if a vendor sold goods to the person, they could redeem it to the issuing institution for the agreed price. This kind of thing is in fact the origin of the concept of “currency”: coin and paper money are literally just MacGuffins that we collectively agree to pretend have intrinsic value so that we don’t have to rely on straight barter. In other words, a farmer probably has a use for a case of nails, but the smith making the nails might not have an immediate use for a bushel of potatoes, so instead the farmer sells his potatoes to the townsfolk writ large for money and then uses that money to buy the nails. Banking, too, is pretty basic. Rather than keep their money in a safe, merchants hand extra money that they don’t need immediately to a banker to hold onto. The banker, knowing that the depositor doesn’t need his money immediately, can then loan that money out to people who do need it, profit off of the interest, and then pay some of that interest back to the depositor as a fee for the use of their money. He can also issue a letter of credit that people can take to financial institutions elsewhere. None of this requires advanced technology, and in fact all modern electronic banking has really done is automate a lot of it. It is, however, very dependent on people and institutions trusting each other: in eras when the majority of people were illiterate, one’s sworn word and reputation were extremely important. Official seals and signatures counted for a lot, but so did handshakes and promises. And for what it’s worth, Spice & Wolf also covers a lot of pre-electricity methods of fraud. Remember: stuff is worth what you can get people to pay for it. No more, and no less. Here’s some modifications you can make for a D&D game. Priests of Abadar[1]

Question: As a Dungeon Master, would you let a player choose to lower an ability score to fit their story?
Answer: Yes, but. The “but” is the cardinal rule of tabletop gaming and other group leisure activities: “Play so that everybody has fun.” While you do want some variety in your PCs, you probably do want them to be roughly comparable in ability score spread. And the fog of war can interfere with whatever fun they thought a deliberately gimped PC might be: depending on your gamemastering choices, the other players may end up having to carry them through many fights, which usually isn’t enjoyable for them, and not being able to contribute might not be fun for the player. Personal story time. I haven’t run a party with a deliberately gimped PC, but I have played in one. My second campaign with my current group was a “gunpowder fantasy” world (circa 1700), with us playing in essentially the Mediterranean and Aegean of the setting. My friend played a 700-year-old elf witch who went by “Granny Elfwin”. She was actually the matriarch of a significant noble family who ran away from the elven lands to have some adventures in her twilight years, and happened to be my half-elf ranger/gunslinger’s biological great-grandmother via a peasant girl one of her grandsons knocked up. Art by Vahid Naderi By Pathfinder rules, being 700 puts her in the “venerable” age category, meaning a total -6 to all physical stats in exchange for +3 to all mental stats.[1] Buddy knew going in it was a deliberately gimped character but they liked the idea of Granny’s “crazy cat lady” persona too much. And to their credit, Granny was fun to have around out of combat, and there were some great gameplay moments, like when she used her flight hex and a sack of alchemist’s fire to basically napalm a pirate anchorage, and the slumber hex meant more uses of coup-de-grace than I’ve ever seen in any campaign. The gameplay problems really only cropped up later in the campaign. As designed, the Witch is mostly a debuffer reliant on Will save-or-sucks. Which is not a bad thing: there’s an idiom in 3.X that a failed Reflex save will hurt you, a failed Fortitude save might kill you, but a failed Will save might be a TPK. Unfortunately, two major categories of recurring enemies turned out to be completely invulnerable to a bunch of her best tricks: the gargouilles de la mer (homebrew fishmen) were immune to sleep so weren’t affected by her slumber hex, and the villainous Archduchy of Trapyzion trying to reconquer their old empire used a lot of constructs which were naturally immune to most of her spell list. Second, being a full caster to begin with and because of the age-related reductions in her physical stats, Granny was essentially no use at all in a physical contest: she had to hope that the frontline—my ranger/gunslinger, the gnoll brawler, and the druid’s carnivorous plant companion, and later a bloodrager cohort after Granny took Leadership (one of my various half-siblings, my bio father having sown his wild oats quite far and wide indeed)—could keep the baddies off her. Which wasn’t always successful. Thirdly, the dicebot seemed to hate Granny after a while. Fully buffed, I could lay down more single-target DPS with a brace of pistols than the party wizard (touch attacks FTW), whereas there were a lot of fights where Granny struggled to do anything useful at all because even when we were up against something Granny could affect, they practically always rolled high and passed her save DCs. Buddy’s going to be playing a more conventional character (sword-and-board samurai) in my game.

Question: In the U.S. presidential elections, do voters have the right to directly vote against candidates they dislike? Do voters have the right to express their opposition to disliked candidates by not casting supportive votes for other candidates？Yes or no?
Answer: Yes and no. You can't directly put a -1 vote in a candidate's column. You have to vote for a candidate, any candidate if you want to vote in a given race at all. That being said, there's a couple of other options. Door number one, you can just leave a race where you don't like any of the candidates blank. Your ballot for the other races will still be counted. Door number two, if you want to slightly screw over a particular major party candidate, you can vote for the third party candidate closest to their positions. Because we have a first-past-the-post voting system in most states, a percent of the total that goes to another candidate can tip an election (though single votes rarely are decisive). Want better? Advocate for ranked-choice balloting.

Question: What is the name of the river flowing through your area?

The Haw River in central North Carolina travels about 110 miles from just north of Greensboro to southeastern Chatham County, where it joins up with the Deep River to flow to the Atlantic as the Cape Fear. The name is short for “Saxapahaw”, an Anglicization of “Sissipahaw”, a now-extinct Catawban-speaking tribe of First Nations that originally lived in the vicinity of modern-day Saxapahaw, NC. Question: What level would a party of 5 need to be at to defeat an adult green dragon? Relatively new DM here, and I'm writing a short campaign and plan for the BBEG to be a green dragon, but I'm not sure what level would be ideal for the players?
Answer: That’s what Challenge Rating is for. Challenge Ratings were introduced as a gamemastering aid in 3rd Edition. The game difficulty is scaled for a party of four, since the stereotypical D&D party generally consists of a tanky melee fighter, a nuker, a healer, and a skillmonkey (stereotypically fighter, wizard/magic user, cleric, rogue/thief). The Challenge Rating for a creature is meant to represent a reasonable fight for a party of four characters of level equal to the CR, but it is always possible, though risky, to throw stronger encounters at your PCs.[1] If you have more than four PCs, you can generally de-rate the CR of an encounter, because more PCs mean additional targets for the encounter to deal with and additional actions to receive. From experience, each additional PC is a difficulty reduction of about 1/2 to 1 CR grade. An adult green dragon is a CR 15 encounter,[2] so I would say that for a 5-member party, 10th level is the absolute bare minimum. More realistically I would leave it for 12th level even as a boss encounter.

Question: In Dungeons & Dragons 5th edition, Oathbreaker Paladins are required to be evil. Couldn't an Oathbreaker being be good if the oath they broke was with tenants that revolved obedience or violence, such as Conquest, Vengeance, or Crown?
Answer: No, but not for the reason you think. Read the actual text of the class, not the name, and seriously ask yourself whether it describes a person who could possibly not be evil. An oathbreaker is a paladin who breaks their sacred oaths to pursue some dark ambition or serve an evil power. Whatever light burned in the paladin's heart been extinguished. Only darkness remains. Channel Divinity When you take this oath at 3rd level, you gain the following two Channel Divinity options. Aura of Hate Starting at 7th level you, as well any fiends and undead within 10 feet of you, gain a bonus to melee weapon damage rolls equal to your Charisma modifier (minimum of +1). A creature can benefit from this feature from only one paladin at a time. At 18th level, the range of this aura increases to 30 feet. Supernatural Resistance At 15th level, you gain resistance to bludgeoning, piercing, and slashing damage from nonmagical weapons. Dread Lord At 20th level, you can, as an action, surround yourself with an aura of gloom that lasts for 1 minute. The aura reduces any bright light in a 30-foot radius around you to dim light. Whenever an enemy that is frightened by you starts its turn in the aura, it takes 4d10 psychic damage. Additionally, you and any creatures of your choosing in the aura are draped in deeper shadow. Creatures that rely on sight have disadvantage on attack rolls against creatures draped in this shadow. While the aura lasts, you can use a bonus action on your turn to cause the shadows in the aura to attack one creature. Make a melee spell attack against the target. If the attack hits, the target takes necrotic damage equal to 3d10 + your Charisma modifier. After activating the aura, you can't do so again until you finish a long rest.[1] Sure as hell doesn’t sound like a non-evil character to me. The problem, honestly, is that the subclass is misnamed. In previous editions, this concept was called the “Blackguard” or the “Antipaladin”. Unfortunately the writers of the Fifth Edition Dungeon Master’s Guide didn’t properly think through what they were putting to paper: they apparently still considered the “default” paladin to be the older Lawful Good archetype, which is covered by the Oath of Devotion, and therefore an “evil paladin” must have fallen from goodness. A classic canonical example of this is the Forgotten Realms character Scyllua Darkhope: formerly a paladin of Tyr, she now serves Bane. They just didn’t think about the fact that it was now possible for a paladin to begin gameplay as an evil character, a la the unnamed Iconic Antipaladin in Pathfinder 1e. So, if you want to have an evil paladin ascend to goodness in 5e, you need to use a different subclass such as Oath of Devotion or Oath of Redemption. This would be much like how Pathfinder’s Iconic Paladin Seelah was once a thief who stole the helmet of a paladin to sell for food, only for that paladin to then die from a head injury while defending the city from gnolls, prompting Seelah to become a paladin herself to atone for the other woman’s death.

Question: How do you use time as part of your Dungeons and Dragons or other TTRPG campaigns? Timed puzzles? Impending doom when the sands of the hour glass run out? World altering changes at sunset?
Answer: The first act of my upcoming Pathfinder campaign is mostly mapped out at this point. The players are going to start in the settlement of Khoka in eastern Qadira and hire on as caravan guards with the family of a man named Wafiq al-Kazemi, who works the trade roads of Casmaron with camel and horse. Al-Kazemi’s final destination is the Kelish capital city of Isfahel, which is not detailed in any official source and therefore I made out of a mashup of Persepolis and Istanbul. Since Kelesh is basically the Persian Empire in canon (with some Abbasid Arabia and Ottoman Turkey for flavor), I went to Google Maps and used the distance from Jerusalem to Tehran as a proxy: about 1,100 miles. At an average traveling speed of 3 mph for 8 hours a day (traveling in the morning and evening and resting during the midday heat), you can go about 22 miles a day. I estimated that the major cities on the Golden Path would be roughly equally spaced about 8 days and 180 miles apart, which gives five satrapies to pass through between Qadira and the Imperial Lands (the Achmaenid Empire had twenty satrapies altogether). And since the caravanners want to make money on the way, they’ll stop for a couple of days in each city, which gives the party time to get up to the usual mischief. I have a calendar extension installed in my Obsidian vault to help me keep track of all this by the way. This is the surface level. Beneath the surface, there are a series of timed events going on the background. The campaign starts four days into the official mourning period following the sudden but not entirely unexpected death of the emperor of Kelesh, Padishah Kalish XXII. The funeral procession of Ottoman Sultan Suleyman the Magnificent. However, the start date of the campaign, 5 Pharast, happens to be a holy day for the goddess of the dead in Lost Omens canon, which allows me to start setting up some of the factions that are going to come out of the woodwork. Chief among them, the Cult of the Dawnflower, militant followers of the goddess Sarenrae who care rather more about her being a goddess of the sun and fire and the de facto patron goddess of Kelesh than about her being a goddess of healing and redemption. A clash between them and the Pharasmins celebrating the Day of Bones provides me a wedge that could get the PCs noticed by an employment agent I have set up. Furthermore, other timed events are happening in the background. Kelesh operates on a quasi-open form of succession: while the incumbent usually appoints an heir, any living member of the royal family is potentially a candidate if they can gain the support of the Imperial court, and, Kelesh being significantly more matriarchal than the real-world cultures it’s based on, the word of the queen holds significant sway. In canon, there is an heir designate, Yaril, but he is disliked by Queen Shubat: besides the fact he was born of a relatively recently acquired concubine and not her, he apparently has some behavioral faults. The players are going to get to meet my OC candidate for the throne on the journey to Kelesh—he was out of town adventuring at the time of his father’s death—and he will have secured the necessary support to be unexpectedly coronated by the time they arrive in Isfahel. Which given his personality means all hell’s about to break loose in the deserts and steppes of Casmaron.

Answer: Of course they can have children of their own. “Our” Mandalorian, Din Djarin, is a member of a specific extremist cult, the Children of the Watch, that forbids its members to ever remove their armor in front of another person. That basically precludes sex. So they adopt orphans to keep themselves going. The majority of Mandalorians don't have as strict an interpretation of the Way, and remove their armor all the time, so they're able to have children naturally. Adoption for them is a choice, just like it is for real world people.

Question: If you had been given free reign over The Clone Wars by George Lucas himself (no limits), how would you have written it out?
Answer: I’m going to begin with the assumption that the start and end points have to be basically the same as the original timeline (OTL). In which case, this is the major change I’d make, because it’s my major beef with the way the conflict is presented in canon. Have the Jedi address the sins of the Republic. The Republic in the prequels is comically corrupt and evil, as I’ve discussed in multiple previous answers. This is driven home by the fact that they literally bought and paid for a billions-strong slave army, violating their own stated laws against slavery, because they couldn’t stand the idea that people might want to say “fuck this shit, I’m out”. And the Jedi in canon unquestioningly support this policy. The only ones that don’t, get smeared as dirty stinkin’ Sith or the equivalent. Lookin’ at you, Barriss Offee. And yet we’re still expected to accept that the Republic and the Jedi are the good guys even though they systematically deny basic human rights to billions. You want to know how you present the Jedi and the Republic sympathetically here? Show us the Jedi and the Republic being heroic. Chopping brainless droids in half is easy. Real courage, real morality, is when you hold your own side accountable. So. Show them near-universally reacting with genuine horror at the mere concept of the clone army: not those half-assed "being nice to your slaves" scenes we actually got from Plo Koon et al. in TCW, but actively acknowledging that they are slaves and doing something about it. Show real internal debate over whether they should even be involved with the Republic anymore at all. Show Jedi quitting the Order over it as conscientious objectors, like Bardan Jusik did in the Republic Commando novels, and not turning into bomb-throwing terrorists, Inquisitors, or Sith. “So how do we justify what we are doing now? Breeding men without choice, and without freedom, to fight and die for us? When do the means cease to justify the end? Where is our society heading? Where are our ideals, and what are we without them? If we give in to expedience in this way, where do we draw the line between ourselves and those we find unacceptably evil? I have no answer, Masters. Do you?”[1] And show us others deciding to work internally to try to change minds and mitigate and repair the damage. Hell, one of the main cast members is literally an ex-slave himself and is married to a senator. Instead of leaving Anakin Skywalker’s enslavement as a cheap trick to inspire sympathy for his childhood self, show Anakin and Padmé talking about how wrong this is. Show Padmé sponsoring legislation to emancipate the clones and compensate them for their enslavement. While we’re at it, have her propose sanctioning the Kaminoans for their participation and direct the Republic Judiciary to begin investigating them for crimes against civilization—because according to Lama Su in Attack of the Clones, this isn’t even the first clone army they've made. Obi-Wan Kenobi: Master Sifo-Dyas was killed almost ten years ago. Lama Su: Oh, I'm so sorry to hear that. But I'm sure he would have been proud of the army we've built for him. Obi-Wan: The army? Lama Su: Yes, a clone army. And, I must say, one of the finest we've ever created.[2] You can still have the same endpoint, and it makes Sidious’s victory an even bigger tragedy than before: now the biochipped clones don’t gun down their slave overseers, but rather the people who were actively trying to make them whole. Lucasfilm did none of that, before or after Disney. They just told us the Jedi were “the good guys” and “had no choice”. Just like Lando “had no choice” but to betray Han on Cloud City. Remember what Leia and Chewbacca thought of that excuse? Sorry about the fan edit, I couldn’t find the original clip. Out here in the real world, one of the fundamental principles of the rule of law is that a superior, no matter if they’re a sergeant, a butterbar lieutenant, a general, or the President of the godsdamned United States, cannot arbitrarily order you to violate the law purely on their own say-so. It’s not allowed, and cannot be allowed. And this isn’t even a new idea: it’s existed in the common law since the 1400s at least. And it’s not a foreign idea to science fiction, either. Exhibit A: Star Trek. Exhibit B: Babylon 5. But apparently George Lucas and Dave Filoni never got that memo. In one movie they talk up the Republic’s antislavery laws, and in the next the entire Republic’s governing structure, Jedi and all, nods along approvingly as billions of slaves march into ships to fight their war for them. Simply put, in Attack of the Clones and The Clone Wars, Lucas and Filoni took “the guardians of peace and justice in the Old Republic”, and turned them into villains as bad as Sith: they took the “quicker, easier, more seductive” route of simply bowing their heads and nodding along when tyranny gave them their marching orders. At least Sheev Palpatine never pretended he was the hero, not to the audience.

Question: Why do Westerners like to eat the meat of pigs, a ḥarām animal, and use its fur?
Answer: I've got a pet theory that nearly all religious dietary prohibitions can be traced to a mundane cause. Humans are good at pattern recognition, not so much at intuiting causation for those patterns. This is one of those cases. Like humans, pigs are opportunistic omnivores, and this can mean they’re somewhat more prone than pure herbivores to pick up parasites. In particular, trichinosis, an infection caused by roundworms. There’s a few others[1] but trichinosis is the most common. And humans that eat infected animals can catch the infection. It’s not likely to outright kill you but it’s extremely unpleasant, and prehistoric humans didn’t have medicines that can cure it. But it turns out there’s a very simple countermeasure: cooking. The Trichinella cysts (eggs, basically) can’t take the heat, so even infected meat is perfectly safe to eat if cooked through. Prehistoric Europeans and Asians figured this out, the ancestors of Arabs and Jews apparently didn’t. This isn’t an issue with most meats, but pork can be tricky to cook well: pork loin in particular is very lean and can easily end up dry and tasting like chalk. It needs liquid around it during cooking to taste good: we’ve got a recipe at home where you pressure-cook it in a sauce made with wine and bacon grease. So, in other words, parasitic infections + hard to cook = haraam and kosher. That’s my theory and I’m sticking to it.

Question: I saw the movie Pearl Harbor (2001) and after the attack somebody on FDR's staff claimed if Japan invaded right now they would get to Chicago before they could be stopped. Is that even remotely true?
Answer: Not in the slightest. Pearl Harbor was a stroke of genius at a tactical level. What it wasn't was a prelude to invasion of the continental United States, and everybody at the time knew it. Japan had neither the interest nor the capability to launch a trans-Pacific invasion. Pearl Harbor was just a raid, intended to knock the US Pacific Fleet out of the war before it could properly start. And getting there was a major logistical headache that involved bringing dozens of oil tankers along to refuel the fleet en route. Furthermore, Japan's imperial ambitions all lay in Asia. The US and its European allies were just in the way: in fact they had considered us allies until we took exception to their invasion of China—a fellow member of the League of Nations until Japan rage-quit over being sanctioned unless they withdrew. Even if they did get here, occupying the West Coast was about as far as they'd get. The interstate highway system was still decades away: most east-west transport was either by rail or by sea, and most of the western US remains virtually unpopulated to this day. And getting over the mountains and deserts would have been a nightmare: we could supply everything our army needed east of the Rockies and trade land for time until we could bring our vastly larger population and industrial base to bear.
