Question: In Dungeons and Dragons, why would players choose to use weapons with lower damage die, like a dagger or club?
Answer: Could be any number of reasons. For example, a backup weapon. Fiorina Mazzanti uses a glaive (d10, x3 crit modifier) as her primary weapon. However, our current campaign, War for the Crown, involves a lot of politicking, and it’s often not appropriate to bring a polearm along. So, I also gave her a rapier (d6, 18–20 crit range) as a sidearm, which is appropriate to wear in social situations without requiring her to go to fisticuffs. Also it gives me another option in tight quarters: since a glaive is a reach weapon, I can’t use it against an enemy in base contact. This was actually a common set of armaments in the Middle Ages and Renaissance: soldiers would carry a polearm of some sort as their primary weapon but also have a sword as a backup and for close combat. Even as late as the 1700s, the Caroleans of Sweden would wear rapiers with their muskets, as seen in this reenactment. Yes, rapiers: they were real battlefield weapons, not just poncy dueling swords. People sometimes call polearms the “rifles” of the medieval battlefield, not because they’re necessarily deadlier than a one-handed sword, but because they’re indisputably a weapon of war: they’re too cumbersome to carry as a self-defense weapon, a “sidearm”. On the other hand, there’s thematic reasons. As Nesteruk Steel-Tooth, cleric of Pharasma, my main-hand weapon was a longsword (d8/19–20, proficient via an alternate race feature), but I also always had a masterwork dagger (d4/19–20) on my character sheet. The dagger is Pharasma’s favored weapon: she’s goddess of the cycle of life and death, and her priests normally carry a special gray-bladed knife called a “skane”, the hilt of which is embossed with her holy symbol. The skane is a ceremonial tool, used both to sever the umbilical cord in midwifery, and to cut cloth from a roll for burial shrouds. Thematically, consider it something like a kirpan, the distinctive single-edged knife an observant Sikh is supposed to have with them at all times. While it’s a myth that Sikhs aren’t allowed to put it back in the scabbard without it tasting blood, it is an item of great ceremonial importance that should only be drawn for maintenance, to defend oneself or another, or to cut the prasad (a religious food offering). There’s also sometimes builds that require particular weapons or weapon types. Honoré Meunier was my NPC quartermaster during our maritime gunpowder fantasy campaign. When I came to need a statblock for him, I used the Picaroon swashbuckler archetype. Swashbucklers have full proficiency with all martial weapons, but a lot of their class features are much more restrictive and only work if they’re wielding particular weapons. The Picaroon modifies that further by giving them proficiency with one-handed firearms and two-weapon fighting, but the wording of the feature is less straightforward than it seems (emphasis mine): Two-Weapon Finesse (Ex): A picaroon gains the benefits of the Weapon Finesse feat with light or one-handed piercing melee weapons. She also gains the effects of the Two-Weapon Fighting feat as long as she is wielding a light or one-handed piercing melee weapon in one hand and one-handed firearm in the other hand. This ability counts as having both the Weapon Finesse and Two-Weapon Fighting feats for the purposes of meeting feat requirements. This ability replaces swashbuckler finesse.[1] Rapiers are one-handed piercing weapons, but not light weapons,[2] nor is a flintlock pistol.[3] This means you actually can’t get the full benefits of Two-Weapon Fighting with a Picaroon if you use a full-size one-handed piercing weapon: you would take a -4 penalty to attack rolls for both weapons, not a -2 penalty. So I gave Honoré a short sword (d6/19–20) instead of a rapier (d6/18–20), and flavored it as a smallsword. This made it, by the rules, the “light” offhand weapon to the pistol’s full-size one-handed weapon, qualifying it for the full reduction to attack roll penalties. It’s also a real combination sometimes used by period military officers.[4]

Question: Why did they allow Odo to stay on Deep Space Nine during the Dominion War, despite being a Changeling?
Answer: Why not? Starfleet and the Federation knew full well whose side Odo was on, and it wasn't the Dominion’s. While the Federation is by no means perfect and hasn't completely gotten rid of bigotry (augments, androids, holograms), they at least usually don't judge people purely based on their species. As it was, he was a good source of information on changeling biology and was willing to cooperate, which made him an invaluable counterintelligence asset. Furthermore, even if they didn't want him around, Starfleet doesn't have any practical authority over him. Odo generally obeys Captain Sisko out of respect, but he is not a Starfleet officer, he's an officer of the Militia of the Republic of Bajor. And Deep Space 9 is legally a Bajoran territorial possession, which Starfleet operates on the Bajoran government's behalf in exchange for getting to use it as a forward operating base. The Bajorans, too, generally trust him and like him—much more than they generally trust or like the Federation—so they're sure to raise Hell if the Federation takes issue with his presence.

Question: Why did Darth Bane come up with the rule of two because, in my opinion, he acted foolishly and foolishly killing so many powerful allies on the way to rule the Galaxy?
Answer: Because he was an asshole. I mean it, that’s literally the answer. Bane came to the Sith Empire during the New Sith Wars. Previously, the Empire had gradually balkanized between various rival Sith Lords after the destruction of Darth Vitiate, the Sith Emperor, during the Zakuul conflict. Darth Vitiate, in his three main guises: Tenebrae, Warlord of Nathema, Emperor Valkorion of Zakuul, and the face he presented to the Sith Empire during and after the First Great Galactic War. Roughly a thousand years before the films, the renegade Jedi Master Skere Kaan managed to reunify the Empire and reorganized the Sith as the so-called Brotherhood of Darkness. Lord Kaan’s reforms included abolishing the title of “Darth” (a probably-Rakatan word meaning either “emperor” or “immortal”), which he viewed as an attractive nuisance, and came down hard on any attempts by Sith to backstab one another. The dark side is addictive and normally makes people power-hungry and paranoid, but having been raised a Jedi, Kaan understood the value of teamwork, and under his leadership the Sith Empire was, after an approximately thousand-year interregnum, able to take the fight to the Republic again. Understand, he was still definitely a darksider, just a grayer one than most: he believed, as Darth Marr and Darth Krovos had millennia earlier, that Sith needed to be able to work together in order to effectively combat the Jedi, and presented himself as first among equals. Under his leadership, the Sith Empire had pushed the Republic into the bloodiest conflict in millennia and was giving as good as it got. Bane, a former cortosis miner born Dessel of Apatros, defected to the Empire after getting into legal trouble with the Republic and was inducted into the Sith after he was discovered to be Force-sensitive, and adopted the moniker “Bane” after his abusive father calling him “the bane of my existence”. Having had to be self-reliant to a fault in his former business, where he had to be ready at any time to protect his cortosis claims from claim-jumpers, he didn’t get along with Skere Kaan from the beginning. He delved deeply into the lore of the ancient Sith and came up with a different solution: the Rule of Two, an extremist interpretation of a notion he found in the holocron of Darth Revan. That Revan had recorded this while under the influence of Darth Vitiate, a sociopathic Sith spirit who sought only to consume all life in the galaxy and rule over the ashes, and had later returned to the light side, didn’t enter into his calculations at all: Bane saw only power for himself and viewed Kaan and his followers as weaklings unworthy of the name ‘Sith’. By now the Jedi had changed tactics: Master Hoth spearheaded a campaign called the “Army of Light”, a force of hundreds of Jedi meant to force the Sith themselves to take the battlefield on a front they couldn’t afford not to defend, which happened to be the planet Ruusan. They were winning, at a terrible cost, but it was making Kaan and his followers desperate, which was when Bane, now openly calling himself “Darth Bane”, sprung his trap. He taught Kaan about a Sith ritual called a “thought bomb”, saying it would destroy the Army of Light. It did. It also destroyed all the Sith who took part (soul-trapped them, really), which was most of the Brotherhood, and wiped out nearly all life on Ruusan in the bargain. Bane himself killed the few Sith that were left, including the Battlemaster, and went into hiding with his new apprentice Darth Zannah, letting the Jedi think the Sith were extinct. The Republic bought the ruse, enacted a new constitution, and abolished its military. Now, Bane’s original idea was that Zannah was supposed to learn all she could from him, then kill him when she was strong enough and train her own apprentice to do the same. But when push came to shove, he fell back on his old habits. In his fifties, his body began to succumb to decrepitude decades early due to dark side corruption. And he started to worry that Zannah was going to wait for him to die of old age rather than overthrow him, so he abandoned her and went looking for a new apprentice, who turned out to be an Iktotchi bounty hunter. But when Zannah caught up with him, it turned out she just hadn’t picked her own apprentice yet, which he’d have known if his darkside-corrupted ass had bothered to ask. The Huntress agreed to go with whichever of them won, and Bane and Zannah faced off in single combat on Ambria. Zannah got the upper hand, and at the last minute Bane tried to betray her just like he’d betrayed Lord Kaan, this time with the Sith ritual of essence transfer: in other words, he tried to take her younger and still-healthy body for his own. She repelled the attempt and that was the end of Darth Bane. So yeah. Bane was no visionary, he was just a power-hungry asshole.

Question: Do liberals understand that even with Top Secret security clearance you still can’t view TS material unless you have also been granted access? That means that Biden’s lawyers also violated the law by viewing any TS documents.
Answer: I’ve been trained on compartmented information by two different employers (one private, one federal) and currently hold a Secret clearance. Let me explain to you how this works as somebody who actually understands what they’re talking about. Inadvertent possession of classified information is not a crime. Nor is possessing classified information that you have permission and employment-related need to possess. Former Vice President Joe Biden and former Vice President Mike Pence both found themselves inadvertently in possession of a number of a couple dozen classified documents each after leaving office. Shit happens. The government isn’t going to prosecute you for a legitimate mistake as long as you fess up and hand over what you have right away. Both Pence and Biden did so: once they realized what they had, they immediately called the National Archives to have them collected by duly authorized persons. Because of their positions and in the interest of fairness, Attorney General Merrick Garland then opened special counsel investigations into both incidents. At time of writing, Pence has been officially cleared of any wrongdoing, and it’s likely the same will happen with Biden. Former President Donald Trump deliberately took hundreds of boxes of government documents, including over a hundred marked Secret or Top Secret, with him while leaving office, stored them insecurely, showed them off to unauthorized persons up to and including Kid friggin’ Rock, and actively sabotaged his own attorneys’ efforts to comply with the law and return them. That is why his oversized orange ass is in a sling and Biden’s and Pence’s aren’t. It’s not the information he had, it’s what he did with it. As for the attorneys, in order to fulfill their client’s constitutional right to a vigorous legal defense, they have to be able to view the materials for which the government might pursue charges, which fulfills the condition of “need-to-know”. That, incidentally, is why there are so relatively few counts in Trump’s indictment: Special Counsel Jack Smith is only pursuing charges for the couple dozen classified documents that the government can actually afford to have made public as a consequence of the trial. Prosecutors aren’t allowed to try people based on evidence the defense isn't allowed to view for themselves: it’s a violation of due process.

Name: Aaron Davis
Question: Has anyone tried to rewrite the history of the Star Trek universe? Some things just don't make sense and aren't consistent with real life or the rest of the universe.
Answer: Repeatedly. Also, SPOILER WARNING for Strange New Worlds! The problem is you always end up pissing off fans who like the stories the way they were and don't want them retroactively changed just because real life had the audacity to not match fiction, or because the new costuming or VFX team wanted to put their own stamp on it. Us fans generally like the old stuff or else we wouldn’t be fans, and we want the new stuff to build on the old stuff, not treat it as if it’s a burden like the Discovery writers are quoted as doing. At least not without a solid in-universe explanation. Most recently, we had the example of the Eugenics Wars. As originally written in TOS: “Space Seed”, the Eugenics Wars were supposed to have taken place in the 1990s, about thirty years in the future from time of writing. Of course, in real life, that didn’t happen, at least not as described: some of the EU novels took the approach that Khan et al. were background figures of a lot of the post-Cold War brushfire conflicts, you know, Yugoslavia and so on. This is helped by Spock mentioning that the recorded history of the Eugenics Wars is fragmentary at best. Strange New Worlds took a different approach. In the self-titled pilot, Captain Pike has this to say: Pike’s presentation uses stock footage from a number of sources, including both the Maidan revolution in Ukraine and the January 6 Trumpist coup attempt against the US Congress. Pike’s version of events is that “the Eugenics Wars” was just one of several names for the conflict that eventually became known as World War III—something that TOS had been self-contradictory about. This is a good solution to the Eugenics Wars, and it’s a great, dramatic, and thematically appropriate speech: Picard would be proud. But it still leaves Khan and the other augments in a bit of creative limbo (which I can forgive: they’re an extra detail that in context would just confuse matters and detract from the point). Enter “Tomorrow and Tomorrow and Tomorrow”. What Sera alludes to here is the so-called “Temporal Cold War” in Star Trek: Enterprise. It’s a messy and borderline incoherent subplot that was introduced in the pilot basically in an attempt to avoid “prequelitis”: to inject some narrative uncertainty as to whether the Federation would actually form by the end of the series what with various factions from the future using ENT’s present day as a proxy battleground. In practice, much like the rest of ENT, it was chaotic and meandering and never really amounted to much, finally being unceremoniously dropped in the season 4 premiere, at least until Star Trek Online had the bad taste to pick it up again a few years ago. No, I’m not a fan, why do you ask lol. Well, kudos to screenwriters David Reed and Onitra Johnson for taking that manure pile and growing a garden with it. Sera here actually lampshades how little sense the whole thing made: she went back in time to kill Khan before he could rise to power in 1992 and thereby keep the Federation from forming centuries later, only for a bunch of other time travelers to all have similar ideas, clash with each other, and tie the whole timeline in knots—as a consequence of which, she’s been stuck on Earth several decades longer than planned. Add to that, she’s clearly got a few screws loose from being stuck on Earth so long, so even that explanation is subject to interpretation. In one fell swoop, SNW has not only explained away the conspicuous lack of an additional world war in the real 1990s, but simultaneously provided itself and any succeeding Star Trek shows a built-in cover for any continuity gaffes they might happen to make in the future: some time traveler messed with it. Mix in the great double act between Christina Chong as La’an and Paul Wesley as Newest!Kirk, and you’ve got my favorite time travel episode ever, “Trials and Tribble-ations” included.

Question: On the Star Trek universe, are Khan Noonien-Singh and Adam, Arik and Noonien Soong related in any way?
Answer: No. They’re not even the same ethnic group. Singh is a surname of North Indian (predominantly Sikh) origin,[1] Soong is diasporic Chinese (a Romanization of several different similar-sounding Chinese surnames).[2] Incidentally they made a throwaway joke about this in the most recent (at time of writing) episode of Star Trek: Strange New Worlds: in “Tomorrow and Tomorrow and Tomorrow”, La’an Noonien-Singh, a legit descendant of Khan, is mistakenly addressed as “Noonien-Soong” and quickly corrects the other person on the pronunciation.

Name: Aaron Davis
Question: Is there any in-universe evidence that Darth Bane's Rule of Two is simply intended to provide an unbroken chain of biological hosts for Bane's essence?
Answer: None whatsoever. As a matter of fact, this is actually addressed in Darth Bane: Dynasty of Evil. This is Darth Bane about that time: Bear in mind, this is supposed to be a man in his early fifties. Heavy use of the dark side takes a toll, and Bane started to worry in Dynasty of Evil that his current apprentice Darth Zannah planned to just wait until he grew old and decrepit so she’d have an easier time killing him. So he turned on her and started looking for a new apprentice. While he was at it, he started researching the Sith sorcery of “essence transfer” as a backup plan, which Darth Zash had attempted against her apprentice, the future Darth Imperius, many centuries earlier—though that one went quite literally sideways when Imperius’s Dashade bodyguard Khem Val interfered. After some misadventures involving the Huntress, a Force-sensitive Iktotchi bounty hunter who was hired to hunt Bane but ended up being adopted as his new apprentice, Bane and Zannah ended up face-to-face for the last time on Ambria, where it turned out the whole plot of the book was based on Bane’s unjustified paranoia: Zannah fully intended to challenge Bane, she just hadn’t picked her own apprentice yet. So they fought, and Zannah killed him. Bane, more fearful of his own death, required by his own Rule of Two, than he thought he would be, attempted to essence transfer into Zannah at the last second, but, per author Drew Karpyshyn, was unsuccessful. The thing is, the ending of Dynasty of Evil came off more ambiguously to some readers than Karpyshyn intended, so the theory got started that he had demonically possessed Zannah, which then got extended by the theorycrafters all the way down to Sidious. But it was never Karpyshyn’s intention that this be the case.

Name: Aaron Davis
Question: If Sith truly believed in the rule of two, why did they always have secret apprentices and allow dark Jedi (inquisitors) to draw dark side energy?
Answer: Because rules are made to be broken. The Sith never believed in the Rule of Two. Darth Bane himself went looking for a second apprentice late in his life because he became concerned that his then-official apprentice Darth Zannah was insufficiently committed to his ideals and was going to wait for old age and darkside corruption to take him out instead of killing him herself. In fact, Zannah was actually more committed to the idea than the inventor of the Rule of Two was and just hadn’t found a good enough candidate for her own apprentice yet. Bane’s second apprentice, Darth Cognus, agreed to follow whichever of them won, and Zannah killed Bane in single combat. Remember what the Sith Code says: Come on, you didn’t seriously expect that a group whose mission statement is about following passions and breaking chains to always 100% keep to a single rule that requires them to get killed off by their own apprentice, did you? The dark side drives you to paranoia and is ultimately self-destructive, as is the Rule of Two: the Master fears the Apprentice and has an incentive to conceal knowledge so that the Apprentice can’t win against them, and the Apprentice fears that the Master might decide to trade them in on a new model. Both of which encapsulate precisely what happened between Bane, Zannah, and Cognus, the first generation of the Banite Sith, and then again a thousand years later between the final generation of Sidious, Tyranus, and Vader. The Rule of Two was only ever an attempt to channel darksiders’ tendency to backstab each other in a useful direction, and it didn’t even work, not to mention being literally born out of Bane backstabbing the entire Brotherhood of Darkness. Darth Cognus’s first apprentice Darth Millennial quit and started his own Sith splinter group. Darth Tenebrous abandoned it altogether and trained two apprentices, Darth Plagueis and Darth Venamis. And Plagueis’s successor Darth Sidious deliberately picked apprentices who were expendable catspaws and wouldn’t ever be strong or knowledgeable enough to actually defeat him, and backed them up with a veritable army of lesser darksiders—which he called Inquisitors and not Sith because who’s going to stop him? Dead Darth Bane? Dead Darth Plagueis? His quadruple amputee official apprentice? Probably the best summation ever of such things as the Rule of Two was, ironically, given by a lightside Sith: “Forget tradition. ‘The Force shall free me.’ Isn’t that the idea?” — the future Darth Imperius to Darth Thanaton, Star Wars: The Old Republic

Question: Which DnD alignments are not usually allowed by DMs?
Answer: I was hesitant to allow one of my PCs in my side episode series to be a CN Inquisitor of a CE goddess (Lamashtu, for reference). My personal preference for PC alignments lies to the upper left corner of the table: LG, NG, LN, and TN. Outside of that corner there's increasing potential for PVP conflict. Also we had a party that included an LG paladin of Iomedae. Fortunately I took the risk, and I was rewarded with some great player moments. If it had been anybody else I might not have, but he was the GM of our main campaign at the time so I was willing to take the risk on his RP style. In our current campaign I'm playing the paladin, of Shelyn (NG goddess of art, beauty, and love), and he's playing an LE-turned-LN cleric, and amusingly our PCs work surprisingly well together. I'm running the next campaign and I'm letting him play a half-succubus TN cleric because I loved the backstory he came up with and, after playing with him in three campaigns, I trust him not to be disruptive. That's really the core of it. If it's a new or pickup group and you don't know the players well, you're probably best off restricting things to the upper-left corner of the alignment chart. There's always the risk of the guy who wants to play CN or CE being an edgelord who just wants to be a murderhobo and screw with the other PCs. But if you know their RP style and trust them not to make life hell for the other players, you should feel free to open things up.

Question: Stormtroopers in real life are special forces. So what is the normal imperial army like and how do their soldiers look?
Answer: Like this: The word “stormtrooper” is German: originally Sturmtruppen, meaning “shock troops”. The role of Sturmtruppen originates with the Russian Army in World War II during the 1916 Brusilov Offensive, but the Germans copied and perfected it. Their role was to break the deadlock of trench warfare: they were light skirmishers who were trained to infiltrate behind enemy lines and find and break open weak points that subsequent waves of regular infantry could then exploit, allow the army to advance. This was in fact the beginnings of the style of combined arms tactics that became known as blitzkrieg: during the inter-war years, the tactics of the Sturmtruppen were combined with developments in armored warfare and tactical airpower to create the German doctrines of World War II. Stormtroopers in Star Wars do that kind of thing sometimes, as in the opening to A New Hope where the 501st Legion is embarked on Darth Vader’s flagship ISD Devastator. But it’s not their primary role. Rather, the Imperial Stormtrooper Corps’ primary role is one of counterinsurgency, as we see in Rogue One. The Clone Wars officially ended with the coup d’etat by Emperor Palpatine against the Jedi Order and the Senate, but Darth Vader shutting down the droid armies from Mustafar didn’t actually end the fighting. A lot of organics also supported the Separatists, and they’re not going to just stop fighting for independence from Coruscant just because of a change of regime. There were also Republican planets that didn’t join in the “thunderous applause”. So in actual fact, the Imperial regime had to spend at least a decade reconquering and pacifying planets that refused to bend the knee. That’s what the Imperial Army is doing in the scenes from Solo and Andor I linked earlier. Once the conquest is largely completed and a proper puppet regime is installed, the stormtroopers come in. They’re an occupying force: they act as a visual reminder of the Empire’s boot on the galaxy’s neck. Take particular note of their typical equipment compared to GAR clone troopers and Imperial Army forces: They’re all pretty well-armored, good body armor being relatively plentiful in Star Wars. But the clone trooper and the “mudtrooper” are using big, cumbersome weapons that are more suited to field battles than to kicking in doors and fighting in narrow city streets. The stormtrooper’s E-11 rifle is different: short and lightweight enough that it can even be wielded one-handed in a pinch, it’s meant for fighting in much closer quarters. It’s rather like the difference between a full-size M16A2 rifle and the cut-down M4 “carbine”: the M4 sacrifices some range with a shorter barrel, but it’s lighter and fits through doors and hallways more readily. But in the open plains of Afghanistan and Iraq, it meant that that US soldiers sometimes couldn’t even hit the people that were shooting at them, forcing the older M14 to be brought back as a designated marksman rifle. By about ten to fifteen years after Revenge of the Sith, the reconquest of the galaxy is basically finished. The Imperial Army really doesn’t have a role anymore and is also starting to be considered politically unreliable, being largely made up of conscripts and aging Republic-era clones, and the stormtroopers are specialists and volunteers. So the Imperial military is transitioning out of a conquest footing and into a long-term occupation footing. The Rebellion is brewing, but it’s still small and fragmented: people don’t exactly like the Empire, but it’s actually proving better at governing than the prequel-era Republic. And if you don’t get up in their business, they mostly leave you alone. But then this happened. Grand Moff Tarkin unilaterally blew up a Core World to make a point, murdering billions of loyal (or at least not actively rebellious) Imperial citizens in a single instant. Palpatine cackled. The rest of the Imperial government collectively went, “ARE YOU INSANE?????!!!!!!1!” Put simply, the destruction of Alderaan was a public relations disaster for the Empire. Imperial propagandists scrambled to try to mitigate the damage: in Legends they tried to blame it on the Rebels at first, and in both canons they eventually resorted to smearing the people of Alderaan as traitors who had it coming. Stormtroopers lined up ethnic Alderaanians for execution all over the galaxy. But that just made it worse. In a mere four years, half the galaxy had risen up against the Empire. Whole sectors declared independence or called for Palpatine’s removal, and the Alliance Fleet went from a few dozen mostly small ships at Yavin 4, to a true navy by the time of Endor that could take the Imperial Starfleet head-on. The Imperial ground forces, meanwhile, were caught in the middle of transitioning from the conquest mode to the occupation mode and were never properly able to change back. Question: How does Jon Snow have a better claim to the Iron Throne than Daenerys when Daenerys is the Mad King’s direct offspring while Jon Snow is Rhaegar’s bastard?
Answer: Once again, for the people in the back who weren’t listening the first dozen times: Claims are propaganda. They are political statements. Ever heard of Henry Tudor? No? How about King Henry VII of England? Henry Tudor’s last royal ancestor was his great-great-great-grandfather Edward III Plantagenet, who had ruled over a century earlier, via his third son John of Gaunt and John’s mistress Katherine Swynford. Richard II, Edward’s grandson, later legitimized his uncle John of Gaunt along with his cousins by Swynford, but after overthrowing Richard in a palace coup, Henry IV Plantagenet-Lancaster explicitly banned those same lines from taking the throne. Furthermore, Henry Tudor’s connection to the House of Plantagenet came through his mother, Margaret Beaufort, John of Gaunt’s great-granddaughter. In other words, Henry Tudor had essentially no discernible claim to the throne of England whatsoever. In fact, due to some other politicking that stopped John of Gaunt from trying to conquer Castile (he was married to a Castilian princess), the Castilian and Portuguese royal families actually had better theoretical claims than him. And since we’re talking about A Song of Ice and Fire, so did Robert Baratheon, the legitimate maternal great-grandson of Aegon V Targaryen—which is still an incredibly weak claim. Henry Tudor became king the same way Robert Baratheon did: by being the leader of the coalition of English lords that overthrew Richard III Plantagenet-York. To solidify his grip on power, he married into the House of Plantagenet after the fact: his consort was Elizabeth of York, one of the surviving children of Edward IV. But this was little more than a fig leaf to legitimize the revolution in the eyes of people who cared more about lines of descent than about the fact that he wasn’t Richard III. That, not descent or sex, is Daenerys Targaryen’s real problem. All the stuff about claims is BS: it’s an argument that this person or that person should be king because their daddy or granddaddy was king, rather than because their would-be subjects actually want them around. For example: The coalition that forms around Cersei Lannister to defeat Dany is not a pro-Cersei coalition, it’s an anti-Dany one. They don’t particularly like Cersei but they’d rather have her than a foreign invader leading a horde of slaving, pillaging savages. They also didn’t like her father: he tried to rule as absolute monarch but didn’t have the political skill to convince people to go along with it, he just had them killed in horrible manner if they dared gainsay him. As Niccolo Machiavelli observes in The Prince, a ruler should avoid being hated above all else. Oh, Jon Snow? He’s not interested. Therefore his “claim” is completely meaningless. Let’s look at another historical analogy: Sweyn II of Denmark. “Who?” you ask? Him. The grand strategy video game Crusader Kings II actually has an achievement for conquering England as this guy, because believe it or not, he could have been said to have had a claim on the throne at the same time that Harold II Godwinson, Guillaume de Normandie, and Harald III Hardrada were fighting over it. He was the grandson of Sweyn Forkbeard, who was King of England by conquest for five weeks in 1013 AD, and the nephew of Cnut the Great. So yeah, this rando actually had a better theoretical claim than William the Conqueror, whose casus belli was that Edward the Confessor, his first cousin once removed, had promised him the throne and Harold was therefore a usurper. And for that matter, he also had a better claim than Henry Tudor. But unlike the others, he had no interest in pursuing it, so it didn’t mean anything. Jon Snow never wanted the responsibility of being a leader. He didn’t kill Dany for the throne, he killed her to stop her. So any claim he might have from being the biological son of Rhaegar Targaryen is functionally moot. Legally he’s probably a bastard (the annulment argument is really sketchy), but it really doesn’t matter because he doesn’t want the Iron Throne anyway.

Name: Aaron Davis
Question: Do heavy metal bands use backing tracks for their live shows?
Answer: Frequently. This is frankly kind of routine these days. Especially in subgenres like power and melodic metal that use a lot of synth, it’s common for all that to be on a backing track. And it could be as simple as the band not having enough people in it to play all the instruments they want. Powerwolf is a good example. They have a full-time keyboardist, but Charles Greywolf is both the band’s rhythm guitarist and bassist, and tracks the bass for their live performances. This was an intentional decision according to frontman Attila Dorn: they decided as a band that they have a good thing going and don’t want to risk screwing up the interpersonal balance of the group by adding a touring bassist. Sabaton, on the other hand, decided not to get a new keyboardist after Daniel Mÿhr left in 2012. Frontman Joakim Brodén started as a keyboardist (his first instrument was a Hammond B3 organ in fact), and sometimes breaks out a keyboard for certain songs (“The Red Baron” and “Christmas Truce” in particular), but for the most part he’s running around the stage too much. The synth is part of their sound but not the core of it, so tracking it is a good solution. Bloodywood has several multi-instrumentalists in the studio and touring bands, but if they wanted to play everything live they’d practically need an orchestra. So depending on the song, lead guitarist Karan Katiyar will play either a guitar or a flute, Sarthak Pahwa usually plays a dhol or another instrument, and they track the rest. On the other hand, you have groups like Nightwish, where keyboardist Tuomas Holopainen is the core of the sound. They do use tracks, but it’s all manually controlled by him from his triple Korg keyboards: he’s typically playing with one hand and programming with another because he’s just that damn good at it and nitnoid about it. Metal isn’t all one thing. Its diversity is what makes it fun.

Question: In Star Trek: First Contact, how did Picard's crew manage to defeat and destroy the Borg cube that attacked Earth when it was stated in "Q Who" that a single Borg cube could easily destroy a planet?
Answer: Attrition. In DS9: “Emissary” we're shown the battle that we missed back in TNG: “The Best of Both Worlds”. 2368. It’s pretty awful. Those forty starships that were gathered to fight Locutus’s cube? They run straight at it in ones and twos and get picked off piecemeal. With or without having assimilated Picard, this was not a failure of technology: the ships are doing damage to Locutus’s cube. This was a failure of tactics and leadership. Admiral Hanson was fortunate he didn’t live to see himself become a case study in how not to fight the Borg. Starfleet had been the undisputed top dog of two quadrants for almost a century, to the point where most of the Federation practically ignored that the Cardassian border conflict was even happening. And as a result, they got complacent. Also, this is still early TNG, when the Federation would rather screw over its own citizens than fight a war to defend them. Seriously, man, did the same dunderhead negotiate the treaties with the Romulans, Cardassians, and Sheliak, or was that three different dunderheads? Wolf 359 was a major shock to the system. Fearing further Borg incursions, Starfleet reactivated reserves and finished the remaining six Galaxy-class hulls, and they also started thinking seriously about the combatant roles of their ships again, which in the hands of one of the many traumatized survivors of Wolf 359, led to this: While not a true capital ship, the Defiant was a major step in the right direction. But Starfleet was never really committed to the project: they still didn’t want to see themselves as warfighters, and with the Borg threat seeming to have waned, she was mothballed rather than go to the effort of fixing and finishing the promising but deeply flawed prototype. But then this happened. 2371. Looked at one way, first contact with the Dominion was disastrous: Starfleet lost a Galaxy-class starship, the pride of the fleet. But it’s a little more complicated than that. Captain Keogh handled himself surprisingly well: despite his shields being completely ineffective, Keogh maintained control of his crew and his ship and was able to use the Odyssey’s sheer size and power against his enemy. He accomplished his mission and was withdrawing under his own power. The Jem’Hadar had to ram him to actually bring him down. The Galaxy-class and other big ships have proven that they still have a legitimate role in combat if used sensibly, and Starfleet now knows it has to worry about a regional peer adversary for the first time in a century, not just the odd Borg raid. That was the second kick in the ass they needed to get moving in the right direction. The Defiant prototype is pulled from the yard and within a year Chief O’Brien has worked out the remaining kinks, allowing it to be put into proper production, though the class wouldn’t properly enter service for several more years. The mothball fleet is pulled out, refitted and upgraded, recruitment and construction are drastically ramped up, and by the eve of the Dominion War, Starfleet has 30,000 active ships. Thus, the Battle of Sector 001. 2373. Five years after the disaster of Wolf 359, the Borg return, and this time Starfleet is properly ready for them. Starfleet is much larger and much more willing to fight. They swarm the cube, give it more targets than it has guns—letting them rotate in and out for repair and rearmament—and they maintain continuous contact for days. The Borg aren’t perpetual motion machines: their self-repair capabilities aren’t unlimited any more than Starfleet’s, and each cube only has the drones it brought with it and that it picked up on the way. The cube was already on the point of complete shield failure by the time the Enterprise arrived on the scene. Their only real failure was not intercepting the cube soon enough: Picard’s arrival wasn’t some miracle, it was a precision coup de grace delivered when the defenders had run out of space between themselves and their target. Starfleet just wore it out.

Question: Do you think Ainz Ooal Gown is the most interesting Isekai protagonist?
Answer: No. Sorry, but Ainz Ooal Gown is a dime-a-dozen OP MC reskinned as a lich. He’s a completely run-of-the-mill power fantasy protagonist of which there are far too many in the isekai genre. Here are some that are actually worthwhile. Souma Kazuya, How a Realist Hero Rebuilt the Kingdom This man was a humanities undergrad who aspired to the Japanese civil service when he was summoned to another world by a down-on-its-luck kingdom. He has no capability in combat whatsoever: at best he is merely competent with a crossbow. Everything he does, he does through other people: his great gift is the ability to strategize, and to delegate. He solves an incipient famine by hiring a well-traveled man as agriculture and food minister to introduce foodstuffs that had hitherto been overlooked. Since he’s useless on a battlefield, he recruits other people to fight in his stead. He uses his studies of world history and literature, especially Machiavelli’s The Prince (which he frequently quotes from and explains how people misunderstand it) to inform his rulership decisions and create ingenious solutions to problems using the systems that already exist in the world. He also doesn’t dance around his harem for-frickin-ever like every other MC: at present (volume 17) he’s married and a father of five. William G. Maryblood, The Faraway Paladin Will is a shut-in who reincarnates as a baby who is rescued from demons by three undead heroes and is raised to adulthood under their loving care. On his fifteenth birthday, disaster strikes when Stagnate, god of undeath, comes to collect on the deal he made with William’s foster parents. He didn’t figure on their son planting himself between the god and his prey and fighting for their lives. When all seems lost, he’s visited by the long-forgotten goddess of the cycle of samsara who brought him, and swears to fight as her paladin and bring the light of the flame to whomever needs it. This series draws more from the Western fantasy literature that inspired standard Japanese fantasy settings than from its genre-mates: in fact book 3 and 4 are practically The Hobbit with a different set of characters. And rather than lean on RPG mechanics, this series uses a magic system dependent on words and language (rendered as Latin), with clear, consistent rules. It’s also one of the three finest examples I’ve ever found of how a Lawful Good paladin is supposed to be played or written, the others being Paksenarrion Dorthansdotter and Xenk Yendar. William’s spear is not a tool of vengeance, it’s a shield for the innocent and helpless, and he shows mercy whenever it’s possible to redeem a foe. While Will is OP compared to most, there are stronger things than him in this world, especially in the later volumes (the first season of the anime ends at volume 2 but the next season comes out this fall). He also has to learn how to lead other people and think his way through problems rather than trying to bull through with brute strength. Also, no harem. In fact book three has an absolutely hilarious exchange between William and his grandfather the ghostly archmage Gus about that: Gus: On a more serious note, is there really no one? There’s normally something when you go adventuring. You know, like rescuing a strong-minded woman captured by bandits, or gallantly saving a merchant adventurer who lost her bodyguards, or recruiting a dependable swordswoman, or protecting a polite and proper lady of a fallen kingdom. Any number of things. Why are you giving me that look? Will: All of those were guys. Gus: (laughs his ass off) Kagome Higurashi and Inuyasha, Inuyasha Yeah, Rumiko Takahashi’s shounen classic? It’s technically an isekai. You all know the story: seemingly ordinary Japanese schoolgirl Kagome Higurashi falls down a well in the back of her family’s temple, lands in Japan during the Sengoku Period, and gets tangled up with the half-dog demon Inuyasha and a cadre of other wacky companions in their struggles over the Shikon Jewel that Inuyasha’s estranged lover Kikyo took to her funeral pyre fifty years earlier. The series still holds up. Its heroes are superhuman but not so superhuman that muggles can’t reach them.

Question: Do you, or those at your TTRPG table, do a good job making the race of your character distinct (gruff mountain dwarf, snooty high-elf, etc.) or do you just pick the race for the bonuses/traits they get you?
Answer: A little of both. More than anything else, what I’m looking for is a good story I can sink my teeth into. I want to “find out” (i.e. invent) what made this person the way they are. Stats are a consideration but not the primary one: above all else, I want the character sheet to reflect the story I’m telling—and fortunately Pathfinder 1e has enough options that this doesn't usually gimp a character. For example: Mona Wearn being a half-elf gave me a reason why she would leave home and sign on with a privateer: she’s illegitimate, discriminated against by her hometown, and raised on the sea by her fisherman grandfather to keep her out of sight of her fully human stepfather and stepsiblings. The fact that under Pathfinder 1e rules half-elves get a +2 to any one stat (inherited from the human side) is a nice bonus. Fiorina Mazzanti is human because the story seed I used is that she was disowned by her father, a baron, when she got pregnant out of wedlock—and most of the countries of Avistan are human-ruled so that just fell out. I spent the bonus feat on Noble Scion (war) to reflect her upbringing, but getting to use my +4 Cha bonus to roll Initiative checks instead of my +1 Dex bonus sure didn’t hurt anything.

Name: Aaron Davis
Question: Were there any clone battalions without jedi?
Answer: That would be most of them. The usual number given for the Jedi Order’s size on the eve of the Clone Wars was 10,000 personnel. Figure at least half to two-thirds of those were not assigned to the war effort: the other duties of the Jedi aren’t considerate enough to shut up and kriff off just because there’s a war on, and that’s before you get to the Council and the training cadres. So call it 3,000 Jedi deployed with the Grand Army of the Republic, if they deployed the maximum reasonable amount. If we use the numbers from R.A. Salvatore’s Legends novelization, the clone army numbered 1.2 million troops within a month or two after Geonosis (upped to about 3 million by war’s end per the Republic Commando novels). That means there’s approximately one Jedi for every 400 clones—about two companies or one (short) battalion in NATO terms.[1] But Jedi frequently operate in master-apprentice pairs, so that means there’s going to be battalions that don’t have an attached Jedi: rather than one Jedi per battalion, you’re looking at about two Jedi per regiment.[2] The Disney canon supplement Complete Locations upped the numbers to 3.4 million clones.[3] So now we’re at about one Jedi per 1,129 troopers, or a little less than one Jedi per regiment. But then factor master-apprentice pairs: I’m going to arbitrarily multiply it by 1.6 to compensate, so now we’re at one Jedi per 1,805 clones, so you’re looking at roughly two Jedi commanding two regiments, or about five battalions. So no, most battalions in the GAR did not have a Jedi in direct command. And frankly they were better off without some glorified diplomat trying to run into artillery fire swinging a kriffing sword.

Question: How stupid were the Jedi that they never knew that Palpatine was playing both sides? Come on, even a clone found out…
Answer: They weren’t completely clueless. Remember this scene from Attack of the Clones? Realize something interesting here: Most of what Dooku says in this scene is, in fact, literally true. He didn’t have anything to do with Obi-Wan getting arrested (according to one of the junior novels, it was actually Boba Fett who got him caught), Dooku and Qui-Gon Jinn were good friends, and, drumroll, the Senate really is phenomenally corrupt and under the influence of a Sith Lord called Darth Sidious. Dooku is, of course, leaving out that Sidious is his own master and has the civilian identity of Supreme Chancellor Sheev Palpatine, but, as was once said by John Sheridan, it’s always best to plant a lie inside a truth. The Jedi knew full well of the corruption in the Senate, and even though they knew they couldn’t trust Dooku now that he’d revealed himself to likely be a Sith Lord, the suspicion didn’t go away. In Legends, this suspicion eventually bore fruit. James Luceno is in my opinion one of the top five authors of Star Wars novels, along with Timothy Zahn, Aaron Allston (RIP), Michael Stackpole, and Matt Stover, and Labyrinth of Evil is no exception. Remember Obi-Wan mentioning “that business on Cato Neimoidia” in Revenge of the Sith? Well, that’s where this picks up. Obi-Wan and Anakin are leading a ground attack on the homeworld of the Trade Federation, and capture the mobile holoprojector on which Darth Sidious spoke to Nute Gunray back in The Phantom Menace. Because Gunray never fully trusted Sidious, he kept records of all their conversations just in case. Those clues lead Republic and Jedi investigators back to Coruscant, and eventually to the factory in the industrial district where Sidious met Dooku in Attack of the Clones. From there, they followed Sidious’s tracks all the way back to the Chancellery office building—at which point Ol’ Palpypants shits a brick and orders General Grievous to raid Coruscant just to throw them off the scent long enough to finish the plan. (Remember, Sidious was never fully in control of everyone’s fates, he was just really good at improvising new strategies when the Force inevitably expressed an opinion and his plans went wrong.[1]) Couple that with the fact that Sidious’s masking—his concealment of his own Force presence which kept the Jedi from identifying him directly—was also starting to wear thin, likely a result of his near-constant use of battle meditation to shape probabilities to his advantage. “The dark side of the Force surrounds the Chancellor.” — Mace Windu The end result was, even though they weren’t able to confirm that Sidious and Palpatine were one and the same person, they were now pretty sure that Sidious was at a bare minimum somebody pretty close to the Chancellor. And when Anakin informed Master Windu that Palpatine had indeed revealed himself to be Darth Sidious, Windu wasn’t that surprised. “Then our worst fears have been realized.” — Mace Windu It was the worst-case scenario, but it was considered a plausible one.

Question: What happened to Kamino and cloning expirements 10 years after ROTS?
Answer: Legends answer: Nothing. The Kaminoans had been paid and fulfilled their contract, keep to themselves by nature, and are pretty obscure. So they just went quiet and were forgotten. It's not even the only time entire civilizations have fallen off the map: there was extensive contact between the Chiss and the rest of the galaxy in the 4th millennium BBY but after that they went quiet until the prequel era. Disney answer: Nothing. Because something else had already happened to them one year after Revenge of the Sith: they complained to Palpatine that they hadn't been paid for the latest deliveries of clones, so he pulled a Phillip IV on them and had Kamino glassed by the Imperial Navy. It was cheaper than paying them, and had the side benefit of covering up part of the conspiracy that had brought Palpatine to power.

Question: My players are about to go to "court" in the next session. I have "trial by combat" angles covered. What would be some other curve balls for trial methods I could throw at them? Objective for players is to "win" in court, they need a warrant for a rescue attempt.
Answer: I suggest you have a look at the “Social Combat” rules that Paizo developed for Ultimate Intrigue and the War for the Crown campaign—which my group is currently playing so I know them pretty well. Specifically, you want the verbal duel rules. From Ultimate Intrigue: Lem, Iconic Bard, scores points on his estranged brother Meligaster, Iconic Mesmerist. If you’re looking for a warrant, this isn’t really a full trial: you’re really just trying to convince the judge/magistrate/whatever to side in your favor. But this isn’t necessarily a world that runs on modern Western court rules, so perhaps your PCs (Lem) are arguing against opposing counsel (Meligaster), with the judge as the “audience”. Audiences can have biases for or against particular duel tactics, which affects strategy. The basic structure of a verbal duel works like this. Each participant has Determination, which is essentially HP (representing their willingness to continue and how seriously the audience is taking them) and consists of the average of their Int, Wis, and Cha bonuses + their total hit dice. You then begin a series of rounds of trading tactics as opposed skill checks, scored by “ante”, the number of tactics used in a given exchange. Using a tactic to counter the same tactic the opponent just used incurs a -2 penalty on that roll, and winning an exchange with a tactic incurs a cumulative -2 penalty on all uses of that tactic for the remainder of the duel. There’s also various ways to gain “edges”, which can be spent to reroll a given skill check. For example, my paladin Fiorina Mazzanti (Determination 6) was debating a bandit, the Night Swan (Determination 7), who fancied herself an anti-monarchist revolutionary. An exchange went: (The previous is not precisely how that duel actually went, but only because I and the GM were figuring out the rules as we went along and bolloxed them up a few different ways as a consequence.) One of the advantages of doing it this way is that it gives any players who are more inclined to roll-play than role-play a chance to shine in a social situation. Lord knows a lot of D&D players are socially awkward IRL: half the players in my group are on the spectrum, including me. But this way, even our quietest player (who ironically is the on-paper leader of the group IC because the GM made her character Baroness Betony in book 2) got to score some good points when we parleyed with Count Lotheed in a team verbal duel. * The joke I was setting up being, Imperial Betrayal was written by a revolutionary named Hosetter who was later guillotined by his own side when the revolution in question turned into 1790s France and got stuck at that stage for the next 60-odd years.

Question: I bought a 10 year old car with 13 year old tires from a used car dealership and just found out. What, if any, legal action should I take?
Answer: None. This is why you do pre-purchase inspections. I've never owned a vehicle younger than five years old, and most were a lot older than that (my current record-holder is a 1974 Honda CB750). If you bought a car that old, there's almost certainly no warranty: any reasonable person would expect you to know that you're buying the car as-is. That's why you take the car over to your own regular mechanic to have them find everything that's wrong with it before you fork over a single red cent. Some more reputable used car lots, like Sanford Imports where I bought my current 2015 Chevy Equinox, will offer a dealer warranty to fix problems that crop up within a short time of purchase (the dealer fixed a bad axle seal and replaced the rear tires on the Equinox for free, both found by my mechanic before I bought it), but beyond that you're on your own. Furthermore, tires are consumables. Any reasonable person would expect them to wear out and need to be periodically replaced. And tires can be pricey so if the used car lot touched them at all, they probably put on the cheapest rubber they could find. Frankly, you'll probably pay less to just take the L and have new tires put on the car yourself than you would to any lawyer willing to take this case.

Question: In Dungeons and Dragons 5e, can the haste spell be cast on someone who has already be "hasted"? Is there a limit on how many times (assuming it is a different caster, because of concentration)?
Answer: Yes, but it won't help. The general rule in D&D is that unless otherwise specified, modifiers of the same type do not stack. 3rd Edition in particular had a huge list of them, to the point where players of the spinoff game sometimes jokingly call it “Mathfinder". What will happen in this case is that you can cast a second haste spell on a target, but the effect will be the same as if you just had one haste casted. The only thing that will change is when the spell wears off: if the second had a duration longer than the first one, that is when the target will no longer be hasted.

Question: My mom is threatening to take her name off of the co-sign of my car. I pay my payments every month and I paid the majority of the car. Can the car be taken away?

Question: What is your funniest moment in Dungeons and Dragons?

I was basically a walking armory: two swords, four pistols, and a smoothbore musket and rifled musket. One of my swords was this thing (and ignore the part about Achaekek since it was a homebrew setting): We planned to make a two-pronged surprise attack against some mooks in a cavern below us: some of us would go down a shaft on one end of the room we were in, the others would head down a dumbwaiter shaft opposite, which had an enchanted door that had a talking face blocking it. Our GM for this campaign liked wordplay puzzles and the like, and the door borrowed the joke from the Mines of Moria: “Speak ‘friend’ and enter.” The first half of the team heads down the shaft, while Mona’s group prepares to enter the dumbwaiter. Except we miscalculated. The clue wasn’t for us to say ‘friend’ in whatever language. It was to make the door say friend. By this point the other team had engaged the enemy and were outnumbered. So—because Mona had distinctly flexible morality, being a privateer turned pirate—I drew the Fuming Blood Sabre and held it over the door’s face, and spoke the command word to make it drip acid. “We’re in a terrible rush, so say ‘friend’ and I stop this.” The door complied very quickly.

Question: Why didn’t the Empire correct the vulnerability in the Death Star if they knew the Rebels had the design plans?
Answer: Bureaucracy. The Death Star is just a big engineering project, and this kind of stupid thing happens on big engineering projects literally every day: NASA once lost a space probe because somebody forgot to convert units between SAE and metric. Somebody probably did notice the problem, but either didn't think it was worth the trouble to change (any attacker would have to first get through sheets of turbolaser fire and thousands of TIE fighters), or wasn't listened to. There's a subplot in the Legends novel Death Star about exactly this. One of the cast members is an engineer who was shanghaied onto the project, and she notices the problem during construction. And, bear in mind, she's not even thinking it's an avenue of attack, she just thinks it doesn't make engineering sense to have a second exhaust port right underneath the main port, because it's inefficient. So she sends a change order up the line to have what all canon until Rogue One thought was just an honest bantha-kriff fixed. And then she comes back way later and they built it as designed, because for whatever reason her change wasn't finalized. Sometimes, things just break.

Question: Why do you believe a KKK member should be allowed to refuse to bake a cake for a black person due to “sincerely held religious believes?
Answer: I don't. People who support the baker in this are missing the forest for the trees. You see, within the lifetimes of both of my parents, it was legal, even encouraged in much of the United States to put up a sign that said something like this:[1] Oh, you don't see the problem yet? This was a thing, too, and not just in the South:[2] So was this, Murphy Barrett. This one was in Canada, even.[3] It isn't about one cake. That's why the cake baker cannot be allowed to refuse to serve customers based on the color of their skin, religious excuse or otherwise: because one day it's him, the next day it's the whole grocery store, the day after that it's the gas station down the street, and pretty soon it's the whole town. Souma Kazuya, an orphaned university student who aspires to the Japanese civil service, is summoned to another world by the King and Queen of Elfrieden to become the yuusha. He thinks about it for a minute and decides to ask them for more information. Turns out this kingdom has fallen on hard times: public corruption, decaying infrastructure, economic instability, the works. And he makes such a convincing case that they betroth him to their daughter and then abdicate the throne to him. That’s just the first chapter/episode. King Souma (as he becomes known because he signed his name in Eastern name order on a bunch of official documents before figuring out the country uses Western name order) only has a minor magical talent that lets him remotely manipulate objects, which he mostly uses to fill out multiple documents at once. Everything else he does is through administrative and managerial skills: he’s really, really good at figuring out the best way to employ people. He’s also almost completely useless in combat, but fortunately his harem, starting with Crown Princess Liscia, very much isn’t. It’s a dense, multilayered story with impressive worldbuilding and a great protagonist who uses information, guile and diplomacy to overcome his problems instead of being an OP MC who smites everything in his path. Question: How can I run an evil character in D&D?
Answer: I almost always play Good characters, but I’ve thought about this for a backup character should something crazy happen in our War for the Crown run and my paladin dies. The typical mistake people make with an Evil character, and often with Chaotic characters as well, is that they play them in ways that are disruptive. That is, they break the most fundamental rule of any group activity: Play so that everybody has fun. (That was actually a rule of my dad’s that I grew up with.) So, first off, get rid of the idea of playing a Dastardly Whiplash or a Joker, a guy who just does evil shit to people because evil. You have to think of your character as a person, not just a statblock and an alignment, and evil people still have reasons for the things they do. They’re almost certainly bad reasons, I will grant, but they’re reasons nonetheless. This is how you do an evil character well. Star Trek: Deep Space Nine gave us a truly great villain in Gul Dukat (played by Marc Alaimo for seven seasons). He genuinely sees himself as the hero of the story and sincerely believes he’s in the right no matter what he does. He’s also quite intelligent: he’s a good planner and a good tactician. And he has enough sense that he’s willing to work alongside the protagonists when they have mutual interests. But, out of character, he’s evil. He personally ordered the deaths of thousands of people, plotted to murder his own illegitimate daughter that he fathered on a sex slave lest her existence make him look bad (he was only barely talked out of that one), and even handed his own country over to a foreign conqueror so that they’d put him in charge of it. And all that was before he started dicking around with the Pah-Wraiths. He had reasons for all of it, mainly personal power and prestige. They were bad reasons for evil actions, but they were reasons. So, here’s my evil backup PC. Meet Sylmara La’vellathian, CE elf antipaladin (sinsworn reaver) of Calistria. Art reportedly by Sarah Stone, but I can’t find the original. A highly sought-after courtesan, she’s inquisitive, mercurial, vain, vindictive, and merciless. She keeps poison and a hidden blade concealed on her person, and in her backstory, she deliberately injured a man in a nonlethal duel such that he died of an internal injury, over a mere insult. This is all according to the antipaladin code of her goddess. Antipaladins of Calistria do not demand great things of others, but rather seek to emulate the Savored Sting in their manner. Most are women; their ranks are filled with those devoted to bloody vengeance and the shining lusts that spark it. Their tenets include the following adages. Question: WotC has made the OGL 1.0a irrevocable and published 5e's SRD under Creative Commons. Does this affect your opinion of their ability to shepherd the brand?
Answer: Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice, shame on me. This isn’t the first time Hasbro and Wizards of the Coast have tried to throw out the OGL. The previous time was back in the late 2000s: you may not remember this but they didn’t have an OGL for D&D 4th Edition. (You remember 4E, right? Right?) Instead, they had the Gaming System License. This had a couple of bits of corporate evil in it: When the GSL was finally released, it contained a poisoned pill: If you used the GSL, you could not publish anything in the same product line using the OGL. It also contained a termination clause, just like the one used in the D20 System Trademark License: Hasbro could unilaterally cancel the GSL at any time, at which point you would need to immediately de-list your books and pulp your inventory. After more public outcry and pressure, they eventually dropped the poisoned pill. But the termination clause stuck. That was, after all, more or less the whole point of the exercise.[1] This is why there was no significant third-party market for 4E the way there was for 3E: third-party content creators had to choose between editions initially, and frankly 3E was more popular so most didn’t move on to develop for 4E. It also had a major unintended consequence. It is not an exaggeration to say that the GSL led directly to the creation of the #2 tabletop RPG, Pathfinder. Paizo, Inc. was originally founded by Wizards alums to publish the Dungeon and Dragon magazines for them early in 3E, but when their license wasn’t renewed in 2007, they started publishing playable 3.5E campaigns in their own original setting, Golarion (now called the Lost Omens setting). In the face of the delayed rollout of the 4E 3pp license and then the growing evidence that the license terms wouldn’t be 3pp-friendly, they decided to instead publish their own rules update to 3.5E, the Pathfinder Roleplaying Game—which still used the OGL and therefore allowed third-party developers to create their own supplements. I own several myself and borrow from them liberally. Pathfinder ended up outselling 4E, and even though Wizards took the top seat back with 5E, their colossal pooch-screw with the OGL controversy almost caused history to repeat itself: early this year, Paizo sold eight months’ worth of Pathfinder inventory in only two weeks.[2] They are also migrating Pathfinder Second Edition off of the OGL: 2E doesn’t use any version of the Wizards SRD and therefore doesn’t need it; Paizo only retained the language to make life easy for third-party developers. They are collaborating with several major game developers to create the Open RPG Creative License or ORC License, which will be explicitly irrevocable and placed in the care of a nonprofit.[3] They won’t be fooled again. No, no!

Question: Which is best D&D Class for tanking?
Answer: This question relies on a fundamental misconception about D&D: that its gameplay is at all similar to video games. It can be, but it doesn’t have to be. Typically, multiplayer video games with a D&D-style class system have three or so broad categories of character: DPS, tanking, and healing. Star Wars: The Old Republic is a good example of this. Image by Illeva[1] Thing is, tanking isn’t just soaking up damage, it’s soaking up damage and drawing the enemy away from more fragile PCs, which usually uses an aggression mechanic. This works fine in PVE, where you’re fighting AI enemies that are designed to be susceptible to your aggro increase techniques. But just try it against human enemies in PVP. Conceptually, combat in a tabletop RPG has a lot more in common with PVP in an MMORPG than it does with PVE. Your enemies aren’t run by a computer program with preprogrammed attack patterns and specific weaknesses to your “taunt” skill, they’re run by an actual person, the game master. So, what you actually want out of a “tank” is a combination of durability and mobility, because your job is to stay between oncoming enemies and your more fragile teammates such as pure casters. Moreover, you need the tactics to use that effectively. For a very basic example: Art credit: Lucienne “Luce” Leroux by Rama Indra for Celestian Tales: Old North,[2] and Meliya Arkona by Eva Widermann for Pathfinder RPG’s Curse of the Crimson Throne Adventure Path[3] During a combat in part one of War for the Crown, we got ambushed by two groups of enemies coming from two directions in a warehouse. I’m playing a paladin, Oath of the People’s Council (left); the other PC on my side of the battlefield is a psychic bloodline sorcerer (right). Initiative order has me moving ahead of the enemies, so I activate Stirring Monologue and reposition so I’m between them and the sorcerer. This means they can’t get to her without triggering an attack of opportunity and getting a halberd to the face. They go for me, I take a minor hit, and tell the sorc’s player to go help the others, I’ve got this, and lay into the mooks with all the deadly grace a Shelynite paladin can muster.

Question: Is America the only nation that bastardizes foreign cuisines (e.g., California roll, deep-dish pizza, orange chicken, etc.)?
Answer: Not by a long shot. The Kingdom of Portugal had several colonies along the coast of India beginning in the early 1500s: Goa in particular lasted from 1510 to 1961 before being invaded and annexed by the Republic of India.[1] And one of the more interesting things we got out of that was vindaloo. From the Portuguese carne de vinha d'alhos, it began as an attempt to do something with leftover ship’s provisions: meat (carne), usually pork, would be packed in wine vinegar (vinha) and garlic (alho) to preserve it on ocean voyages, and then whatever was left over at the end of the trip to Goa was sold off. Local Goan cooks mixed in their preferred spice blends and cook that horrid preserved meat it into something that actually tasted decent. Over time, other ingredients were added depending on local tastes (the wine vinegar would often be replaced with more-readily-available palm vinegar for example), and “vindaloo” became a common part of South Indian cuisine. The choice of pork itself is a very European thing: due possibly to Muslim influence (the Muslim Mughals ruled India for a couple centuries until the British conquest), most Indians do not consume much pork, but Indian Christians, who make up 25% of the population of Goa, often do. This adaptation of European food into Indian food, then was exported back to Europe through trade routes and, in modern times, curry restaurants, and further adapted to European palates.

Question: If your vehicle gets totaled, are you legally able to take parts from it?
Answer: It depends. I've totaled three cars: two at-fault in rear-end collisions, one where a guy backed into me in the parking lot. Pretty sure I've seen every variation of this. What it comes down to is, do you still own the car? If your car is totaled but you didn't have collision coverage, you probably still own the wreck. I removed the stereo receiver I had installed in my '98 Maxima before selling it to a coworker whose parents needed a parts car. If you did have collision coverage, there's a couple of variations. You can have the insurance company take and dispose of the wreck, or you can ask to keep it. In the case of my '01 RAV4, the car was probably still fixable but the damage was more than it was worth and the car was not drivable (radiator was cracked). I let USAA take the car, and they paid off the loan and sent me the remainder. My '01 Forester, on the other hand, was still drivable: all the damage was to the right-side bodywork, but the car was on the verge of succumbing to jalopyism so it was more than the car was worth to fix it. So USAA paid me and let me keep the car, put the payout and some stimulus checks to buying a new one, and then sold the heap on Craigslist to a guy who knew full well what he was getting and just needed four wheels and an engine in a hurry. On the other hand, my father got into a situation where he managed to total the same car three times in the '80s: the insurance company didn't want to pay to have it fixed, so he took the payout on his Toyota Celica and had it done himself. After the third time, however, the insurance company told him the car absolutely would not be safe to drive even if he had it fixed again: the structure had been crumpled too many times. So they refused to let him keep and fix and just took the car. (It wasn't a huge problem: we were about to move to Australia for the Navy anyway.)

Question: Have you played Call of Cthulhu? How is it different than D&D if you have? If you haven’t, does it look interesting?
Answer: I haven’t played original-flavor Call of Cthulhu; however, I have played its spinoff, Pulp Cthulhu. If the only RPG you’ve ever played is D&D, then be warned that CoC, including Pulp, is very different. There’s no character classes or levels nor do you muck about with a dozen different dice: it all runs on a d10/d100 system along the lines of Fantasy Flight Games’s Warhammer RPGs like Dark Heresy, wherein your character background dictates your basic skillset, and you have to roll a d% and roll lower than the skill or attribute score to succeed at a check. It also uses “degrees of success” (not used in D&D except in influence checks in 3.X): if you roll half your skill score or below, it’s a “Hard Success”, and if you roll one-fifth or below it’s an extreme success. Also, you improve your skills by using them rather than gaining experience points. There’s also the Sanity mechanic, where your character can gradually lose their mind from witnessing eldritch horrors. That said, Pulp has more of the feel of typical D&D gameplay: it’s more of an action-adventure game and has more room for silly player antics, as well as having higher-powered PCs in general. We played several missions of the campaign The Two-Headed Serpent over the summer because one of our Pathfinder players was busy with an internship on alternating Saturdays. Question: How many cops armed with pistols would it take to kill a single Tyranid Gaunt (Warhammer 40K)?
Answer: How many have you got? Joking aside, there’s actually a decent way to answer this. In Warhammer 40,000, a standard handgun is what they would call a “light stubber”. With that particular example, 6.2mm short is comparable to a .25 ACP round, which was generally sold for pocket-sized weapons such as the FN M1905/Colt Model 1908 Vest Pocket (both were based on the same Browning prototype[1]), but it gives you some idea. The stub gun is your average gunpowder-powered projectile handgun. These aren’t used in Warhammer 40,000 wargaming because quite frankly they make the Guard lasgun, a.k.a. the “flashlight”, look like a bazooka.[2] But they do show up in some of the tabletop RPGs. I’ll use Dark Heresy Second Edition since that’s what I have the rulebooks for. The 9mm handgun is a typical cop weapon these days, so we’re looking at a stub automatic. “Pen” is the key stat here: it refers to the weapon’s ability to penetrate armor, which is crucial. Pen (Penetration): Penetration reflects how good the weapon is at cutting through armour. When a shot or blow hits a target, that hit ignores a number of Armour points on that Hit Location equal to the weapon’s penetration value. If this ignores more Armour points than the Hit Location possesses, the hit ignores all Armour and the additional penetration has no effect. For example, if a weapon with a penetration of 3 hits a target with 5 Armour points, the target only counts as having 2 Armour points against any damage the hit causes. Note that penetration has no effect on force fields (see page 168), but it does affect cover. (Core Rulebook p. 144) Tyranids aren’t statted in the Dark Heresy rulebooks, but they do appear in the sister game Deathwatch which has similar rules (the main difference is that DH tends to have lower-powered PCs). Both termagants and hormagaunts have 9 Wounds, 3 Toughness and 3 armor points across all body parts.[3] 1d10+3 Impact damage - 3 Toughness - 3 Armor = 2.5 average damage per hit, so on average you’ll need to hit the gaunt four times before you can start inflicting Critical Damage, which is required to actually kill it. So it could be as little as five shots if you roll well on the crit table. One guy with an automatic can’t do this in one round: if you spend a full-round action firing semiauto, you’ll only get three shots off, so that’s at least two guys, if you hit every time. So now we’re down to movement speed and firing range. Termagants are pretty slow, but hormagaunts can cover the maximum range of a stub automatic in two turns. So I’d probably want at least six cops to one ‘gaunt. And of course, you never get just one termagant. EDIT 02/08: I stuffed up the rules in my original version of this, forgot to account for the Toughness bonus.

Question: How long are Tolkien's leagues, i.e., how far did Wingfoot and his companions run?
Answer: A league is a historical unit of measurement. 45 leagues is 135 miles. This means, unfortunately, that Aragorn's feat is not nearly as impressive as it sounds. Covering that distance in three days, 72 hours, means that Aragorn was traveling an average speed of 1.875 miles per hour. You probably walked faster to the fridge the last time you got up to get a snack. Snailfoot would have been a more appropriate nickname. Just a reminder that Tolkien was an English professor, not a math teacher.

Question: In Top Gun Maverick, why didn't they use 5th generation jets to accomplish that mission instead of using old technology against Su-57?
Answer: Because then it wouldn't be a Top Gun film. The in-universe reason given is that the F-35C wasn't approved yet to drop the laser-guided munitions used in the attack, and GPS jamming prevented the use of GPS-guided weapons. As David Tussey notes in his answer, this is a pretty threadbare excuse. There's really no good reason the F-35C couldn't have been used here. In fact, the sanest way to do the mission wouldn't have involved the Navy at all: they could have flown a B-2 Spirit out to a nearby airfield and gotten in and out without having to take the canyon route. For example, assuming the mystery country is supposed to be Iran (I've been calling it Fubaristan, but there's only so many countries hostile to the US that have a nuclear program and an air force that is both competent and Russian-supplied), our bases in Bahrain are well within range. But then it wouldn't be a Top Gun film. The movie was a passion project of Tom Cruise, who wanted to film with real Navy aircraft just like the first film. And there's a pretty big technical glitch with the F-35C. Besides the fact it probably wasn't available in sufficient numbers to film with (it only entered service in 2019, and the production of the film was delayed by the pandemic), you can't use it to film an actor in a real aircraft, because it only seats one. But an F/A-18F, like an F-14, is a two-seater. So they were able to make it look like Tom Cruise was flying an F-18 by sticking him in the back seat of an F/A-18F, normally occupied by the Weapon Systems officer, and then having an actual Navy pilot do his level best to make him lose his lunch.
