Question: Have you ever converted a TTRPG character from one game system or edition to another? What was the reason? What were the difficulties?
Answer: Many times. I usually run Pathfinder First Edition, which is a derivative of D&D 3.5E. Converting things from 3.5E to Pathfinder is dead easy since the statblocks are almost identical. Paizo even published a free conversion guide, which I’ve used to convert entire adventures in under an hour. For a more involved conversion, let’s look at my Asian steppes campaign, Horse Lords of Casmaron. There’s this thing in central Asia called a balbal. It’s a statue that steppe nomads would build as guardians over their khans’ tombs. Legend has it they would sacrifice prisoners or even the khan’s own guards and bind their souls to the balbals, which would animate to attack anybody who disturbed the tomb. As the blogger I learned of this from put it, The souls of your dead enemies. Bound into stone statues. Placed all around your giant, secret tomb in order to serve you in the afterlife and defend you against intruders. Seldom has real-world history sounded quite so much like a D&D adventure module.[1] The system this blogger uses is OSR, “Old-School Renaissance”, which is a successor to AD&D. There’s no clear-cut system to convert this to Pathfinder, so to emulate something like a balbal, you have to step back a bit to the underlying concepts. It’s a statue animated by an imprisoned soul. Sounds like a construct of some kind, right? Guess what Paizo gave us on page 14 of the Pathfinder RPG Bestiary: animated objects. I made two kinds of balbals. One type is a Medium-sized statue of a Kara warrior, CR 3. Img src: Armorcast[2] Medium size means 2 construction points, which I spent on changing the material to stone and the damage type to slashing. There’s also the trait “Haunted”, which is exactly what it sounds like: you get an additional construction point by writing that the object is inhabited by a malevolent spirit—which means that, unlike a normal construct, it’s also vulnerable to positive energy attacks like undead. The second type I made is Large size, based on a wrestler, because wrestling is next to equestrian as the favorite sport of the steppe peoples. Img src: National Museum of Asian Art[3] Large size means 3 CP and a CR of 5. So, made of stone again, haunted again. This time I gave it grab and constrict attacks to go with the theme. The moral of the story is, if your game system is sufficiently flexible and you can reduce a splat to its core concepts, you can convert just about anything.

Question: As D&D Beyond/Roll20 have several digital only campaign, and Covid has kept people apart, Is the future of D&D destined to become a digital game?
Answer: Say rather that I think digital gaming is a future of D&D. My group formed during the pandemic and has always been online by necessity: we met online through a web forum, and four of our members live in eastern Ireland, I’m in North Carolina, and my buddy who invited me started in New Jersey and is now in Colorado. Online gaming has its advantages, especially if, like me, you live in a rural area and you’re a half hour drive minimum from anywhere important. Before I started playing Pathfinder with this group, I hadn’t played since my brother moved out since I just didn’t know anybody else who played. And if, like me, you have a Swiss cheese brain, it’s also a lot easier to have a dice bot to do the calculations in “Mathfinder” than to have to keep track of all the modifiers you’re stacking by hand. But there’s definitely still value to in-person play. It’s a great way to introduce someone to the hobby, and it’s a lot easier to help a newbie figure out what goes where on their character sheet if you can physically see it. And sometimes I just prefer to have a rulebook in hand, if only because it saves on screen real estate: even with two 16:9 monitors on my home rig, things can get a little cramped between Discord, character sheets, and a browser window or three to look up rules.

Question: If "Balance to the Force" means the absence of the Dark Side, then why was The Son from Clone Wars represented as something that was required for balance?
Answer: Ask yourself this: Who told us that the Mortis “Gods” were “required” for balance? Was it, perhaps, the Mortis “Gods” themselves? Just because somebody says something that they sincerely believe to be true, does not make it so. A lot of people sincerely believe the world is flat and only 5,000 years old and will happily talk your ear off about it, does that make either of those the case? The explicit word of George Lucas on the subject is that the Dark Side of the Force is a cancer on it, and a balanced body is not 50% cancer cells and 50% healthy cells, it’s one without cancer. Everything to the contrary was written by people who wanted to draw a false equivalence between the Jedi and the (stereotypical) Sith, much like Sheev “Darth Sidious” Palpatine does in canon—and similarly relies on the idea that the man who spent the better part of three decades manipulating everybody was actually telling the truth about something for once. Do the prequel Jedi have flaws? Absolutely: I’ll be the first to tell you that there are card-carrying Sith Lords in Star Wars: The Old Republic who are more morally upstanding. But one side being wrong doesn’t automatically make the other side right. The Jedi and the Sith neither are, nor represent, either side of the Force in and of themselves: they’re just two rival religious orders that happen to be strongly associated with the Light and the Dark, nothing more or less. They can both be wrong. And the Mortis “Gods” are just unusually powerful Force-users with delusions of grandeur and have no bearing on the basic nature of the Force whatsoever.
